### 1\. Introduction Cigarette smoke is a complex assemblage of liquid droplets, _i.e._, particulate phase, suspended in a mixture of gases and vapors. The toxicants are dissolved in droplets or vapors or both \ [1\], where the droplets range in variable mean diameter from the nano- (dp < 100 nm) into the sub-micrometer scale (dp = 0.1−1 μm) \ [2\]. Cigarette smoking causes a variety of diseases, primarily lung tumors and deficiencies of the respiratory and cardiovascular system \ [3\]. So far, more than 6,000 compounds have been found in cigarette smoke \ [4\], at least 69 of which are known or probable human carcinogens \ [5\]. More recently, the FDA \ [6\] listed tobacco-smoke constituents which are directly harmful ( _i.e._, all carcinogens and toxicants) and potentially harmful (e.g., nicotine being not only a reproductive toxicant but also addictive). ### 3.1.2. Clinical Investigations Clinical _in vivo_ investigations are based on observations of patients or volunteers, where conclusions are drawn according to statistical analyses of data sets and patients’ records \ [74\]. Clinical investigations are important because tobacco product characterizations should not be limited to comparisons under standardized conditions employing smoking machines (as done in laboratory studies) but should also include anticipated conditions of actual use \ [94\]. As experimental investigations are typically designed at the product level, clinical investigations should be at the individual smoker level and/or population level. Clinical investigations can evaluate the pathology of different toxicants and carcinogens _in vivo_ \ [27, 83, 85, 86, 94\]. Doses are monitored by the analysis of toxic substances or their metabolites in biological fluids ( _i.e._, biomarkers). Such a method is for evaluating human exposure to toxins \ [27\] to determine the retention of toxins in the human body \ [83, 85, 95\]. Clinically, Morawska _et al_. \ [83\] reported the total deposition efficiency (TDE) of 36% with a standard deviation (SD) of 10% for second-hand smoke with a CMD of 183 nm, affecting non-smoking individuals. Mcgrath _et al_. \ [85\] and Dickens _et al_. \ [95\] used biomarkers (solanesol) to calculate the TDE of cigarette smoke in seven volunteer smokers. Van Dijk _et al_. \ [86\] revealed the existence of nanoparticles (dp = 6 nm to 50 nm) in fresh and undiluted tobacco smoke for moderate smoking regiments. The number of nanoparticles ranged from 2.6e+6 per to 8.8e+9 per cigarette. Van Dijk _et al_. \ [86\] discovered that the particle counts decreased for smaller nanoparticles. This may be because the small nanoparticles have a high potential to quickly agglomerate into larger smoke constituents or to disperse into smaller vapor molecules. Schripp _et al_. \ [66\] measured the time-evolution of e-cigarette aerosol-size distribution during consumption under different chamber conditions. Clinical investigations can also provide _in vivo_ airflow measurements during smoking. However, the measurements are costly and complex to perform, and accurate results are difficult to obtain due to the spatial resolution and tissue attenuation limit. Therefore, replicas of human respiratory systems have been used widely for experiments. Additionally, compared to experimental and CF-PD investigations, it is difficult to obtain _in vivo_ local deposition efficiencies and detailed aerosol property variations with time. ### 3.4. Parameters and Mechanisms Influencing the Deposition of Toxicants and Carcinogens As mentioned, the transport and deposition of toxicants and carcinogens of tobacco smoke in the human respiratory systems is a complex process which is influenced by many physical mechanisms. They include coagulation, condensation and evaporation, hygroscopic growth, change in composition, and individual puffing behavior \ [85\]. For conventional cigarette smoke, experimental deposition data sets are consistent with classical predictions \ [110\]. It is known that deposition efficiencies (DE) of tobacco smoke aerosols in the lung (60–80%) are greater than expected when smoke particles are in the 150–250 nm range in terms of count median diameter (CMD) \ [26\]. Until now the mechanisms leading to higher DEs have not been fully addressed. For example, it has been experimentally observed that inhaled cigarette smoke particles may grow from 160.1 ± 6.4 nm in diameter to 238.9 ± 16.5 nm by the time they are exhaled, implying a growth factor of 1.5 \ [85\]. The aerosol size development inside the human respiratory system may play an important role to explain the higher DEs. In general, to improve the understanding of the relationships between toxicants and diseases, the following has to be addressed: Definition of potential health risk criteria coupled with efficient potential harm reductions, as well as physical/chemical mechanisms and parameters that influence the transport and deposition of tobacco smoke aerosols. #### 3.4.1. Variability in Smoking Behavior Inhalation of tobacco smoke aerosols is a multi-step process which consists of puffing, mouth hold, inhalation, and exhalation \ [2, 85, 90, 95, 111\]. Typically, a smoker first draws a puff-of-smoke into the mouth cavity and holds it with the soft palate closed \ [95\]. However, some smokers may inhale the smoke directly into the lung \ [111\]. It is well observed that the puffing behavior ( _i.e._, volume, duration, inter-puff interval, frequency, and waveform profiles) vary substantially among individuals as well as different tobacco products. Different puffing behavior, especially the puffing flow rate will give different transit times of smoke through the shortening length of a cigarette; hence, influencing aerosol size and location distribution, as well as the aerosol composition at the mouth inlet \ [12, 13, 26, 82, 92, 95, 108\]. Influences between puffing behavior and aerosol properties will have a strong impact on the local and total deposition efficiencies in the human respiratory systems. Typical puffing characteristics are \ [108, 111\]: - 31 to 86 mL in puff volume. - 0.9 to 3.0 s in puff duration. - 18 to 64 s for inter-puff interval. - 2,100 to 3,800 mL/min in puff flow rate. - 8 to 16 puffs per cigarette. Twenty-five different puffing regiments generated by idealized smoking machines (see Table 2) to reflect “human puffing behavior” are discussed in Ref. \ [90\]. Although the puffing regiments in Table 2 can be utilized in CF-PD simulations for quick analyses, they may not reflect actual puffing behavior. For example, single puffing waveforms for LHC products and conventional cigarettes are shown in Figure 3(a,b). Generally, LHC products (e.g., e-cigarettes) require stronger puffing than conventional cigarettes (see the discussions in the previous sections). Furthermore, double-puffing waveforms were detected by McGrath _et al_. \ [85\], using a pre-calibrated portable smoking analyzer with seven volunteer smokers. A double-puff profile is shown in Figure 4. For post-puff ventilation behavior, St Charles _et al_. \ [91\] tested 74 established smokers, and reported a mean inhalation volume ranging from 649 to 841 mL, mean lung exposure times from 4.5 to 5.6 s, and a mean inhalation tidal ratio of 1.77. #### 3.4.2. Mechanisms Influencing Time-Evolution of Aerosol Size Mechanisms of inhaled toxic aerosols which may influence aerosol size over time include multi-component droplet/vapor compositions and interactions, condensation and vaporization of droplets/vapors, coagulation effects among particles, droplet-cloud formation and motion, particle charge effect, _etc_. Several of those mechanisms strongly influence the local and total deposition efficiency of toxicants and carcinogens. ##### Evaporation or Hygroscopic Growth Effect The evaporation hygroscopic growth of a droplet is driven by the chemical potential difference of constituent species between the droplet and the surrounding gas phase. The hygroscopic growth of cigarette smoke droplets in the human respiratory system can be significant, and hence may notably alter the behavior and fate of the dispersed phase \ [105\]. For conventional cigarette smoke particles (CSPs), a number of _in vivo, in vitro_ and numerical studies have been performed. For example, Hicks _et al_. \ [112\] reported that the inhaled dense mainstream CSPs may experience a diameter-increase up to 1.7 times at exhalation. Li and Hopke \ [113\] measured an average growth rate of 1.54 for mainstream CSPs with initial diameters ranging from 150 nm to 400 nm at a relative humidity (RH) of 99.5%. Robinson and Yu \ [110, 114\] and Longest and Xi \ [105\] reported an equilibrium growth ratio of 1.4 to 1.7 for mainstream CSPs when the RH approaches 100%. In summary, the hygroscopic growth of conventional CSP is around 1.5 at body temperature and humidity conditions ( _i.e._, T = 37 °C and RH = 99.5%) \ [115\]. The possible size-changes of LHC products may differ from the CSPs \ [12\]. Therefore, the understanding and accurate description of species heat and mass transport processes are key for the simulation of droplet vaporization or growth. There are six groups of CF-PD models based on various assumptions describing the heat and mass transfer associated with real-world evaporation scenarios \ [116\]. Specifically, the CF-PD modeling assumptions for the six groups of mathematical models are as follows. - Group 1: Assuming that the droplet surface temperature is uniform and does not change with time. - Group 2: Assuming that no temperature gradient and species mass fraction gradient exist inside the droplets, _i.e._, infinite thermal conductivity and mass diffusivity in the liquid phase. - Group 3: Taking into account the temperature gradient and mass fraction gradient inside droplets without considering the recirculation inside droplets (Hill’s vortex) which would enhance the effective thermal conductivity of the liquid. - Group 4: Based on the Group 3 conditions, taking into account the recirculation effect by introducing a correction factor to the liquid thermal conductivity. - Group 5: Describing the recirculation effect by simulation of the internal vortex dynamics. - Group 6: Full solution of the multi-phase Navier-Stokes equations. Models of Group 1 are suitable for analytical analysis due to their highly simplified assumptions. Group 5 and Group 6 have not been widely employed because of their complexities and high computational costs. Models of Groups 2 to 4 are widely used in most practical applications. Recently, Zhang _et al_. \ [12\] investigated numerically the size evolution and deposition of conventional cigarette and LHC product droplets in a subject-specific airway model. They validated their numerical model with previous _in-vivo_ and _in-vitro_ studies and found that the hygroscopic growth has no significant impact on droplet size and deposition. Furthermore, Kim _et al_. \ [117\] validated the hygroscopic CF-PD model with experimental data for droplet growth on the submicron scale. They evaluated the hygroscopic effect in the nasal airway of a 5-year-old child for initially mono-disperse 200 nm droplets. Additionally, Sazhin _et al_. \ [118\] developed a kinetic model for droplet heating and evaporation into a high-pressure environment, which takes into account the effects of inelastic collisions, a non-unity evaporation coefficient, and temperature gradients inside the droplets. However, their kinetic model is computationally extremely expensive and hence is presently not suitable for large-scale lung aerosol dynamics simulations. In light of the complex multi-component aerosols in conventional cigarettes and LHC products, the mass transfer for each component may contribute to the total mass change of the droplet. In such a dense air-droplet suspension, particle-particle interactions in terms of Brownian coagulation and cloud formation may occur. Thus, particle-particle interaction must be considered as the primary factor which will cause aerosol size and particle number change, thereby influencing the aerosol transport and deposition in human respiratory systems. For SHS or ETS, as the concentration is not high, interactions between particles can be neglected \ [121\].

Specifically, the cultivation of energy crops such as Miscanthus is justified not only by the need to increase the share of renewable energy sources, but it would make it possible to safely and efficiently manage municipal sewage sludge in agriculture \ [23, 24, 25\]. Miscanthus has a high yield potential within a wide range of environmental conditions and it is characterized by relatively low agronomic requirements. Due to its high resource-use efficiency and tolerance to biotic and abiotic stressors, Miscanthus can be cultivated on marginal land, which plays a minor role in food production \ [26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33\]. It is a crop that improves soil fertility, reduces erosion, has a positive impact on biodiversity and is resistant to diseases and pests. According to Galatsidas et al. (2018) \ [34\], the total area of marginal soils in Europe that can be dedicated to the production of Miscanthus is close to 11 million hectares. At present, the area under Miscanthus is estimated at 19,000 ha in the EU. As shown by many authors \ [35, 36, 37, 38\], Miscanthus can produce a much higher biomass yield after applying a fertilizer, e.g., municipal sewage sludge, which is the source of many valuable nutrients and has a value close to manure, but contains a number of potentially harmful constituents, such as heavy metals or metalloids. The use of municipal sewage sludge could not only increase yields but also positively affect biological and physicochemical properties of the soil profile \ [6, 39, 40\]. That is why the interest in the use of fertilizer in the cultivation of energy crops such as giant Miscanthus has been studied by many authors \ [6, 37, 38, 41, 42, 43, 44, 45\]. The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of the fertilization of municipal sewage sludge on biomass yield and energetic properties of Miscanthus. In addition, the aim was to investigate whether increasing dosages of municipal sewage sludge not only change the properties of Miscanthus but also exert a positive influence on the physical and chemical properties of the soil for biomass production, i.e., changes in soil fertility and the accumulation of heavy metals in soil. ## 2\. Results and Discussion As Miscanthus reaches maximum plant height, it also reaches maximum biomass yield. The end of the growing season of Miscanthus coincides with the onset of lower temperatures, and full maturation and drying of the crop begins with the onset of the first autumn frost, when the first harvest is made. At the end of the growing season, nutrients are translocated from the above-ground parts of the plant to the rhizomes. In older plantations, this process begins in late summer and early fall. The stems are gradually dried during the winter and early spring when they are ready for harvest (if used as solid fuel). During this period, there is a significant reduction in yield (35–45%) due to the dropping of leaves and upper parts of the stem (broom), but also due to the improvement of the fuel properties of the biomass. Field trials have shown that Miscanthus sinensis hybrids yield up to 25 t/ha of dry matter in northern parts of Europe, Miscanthus x giganteus hybrids up to 38 t/ha of dry matter in central and Southern Europe and certain high-yielding Miscanthus sinensis hybrids up to 41 t/ha of dry matter \ [51, 52, 53\]. **Optimizing Nutrient Delivery and Artificial Lighting in Commercial Hydroponic Lettuce Production**  

**Abstract**  
Hydroponic systems for lettuce cultivation have gained prominence in commercial agricultural operations due to their capacity for precise resource management, high-density planting, and year-round production. This paper examines the optimization of nutrient delivery systems and artificial lighting configurations to enhance yield while minimizing pest incidence in controlled indoor environments. Emphasis is placed on the integration of recirculating nutrient solutions, spectral tuning of light-emitting diode (LED) arrays, and environmental monitoring technologies. The findings suggest that targeted adjustments in nutrient composition and light spectra can significantly improve plant growth parameters and reduce susceptibility to common pathogens.  

**1. Introduction**  
Lettuce (Lactuca sativa L.) is a high-value leafy vegetable widely cultivated in hydroponic systems due to its relatively short growth cycle and adaptability to controlled environments. Commercial hydroponics offers advantages over conventional soil-based cultivation, including improved water-use efficiency, reduced land requirements, and diminished reliance on chemical pesticides [1]. However, maximizing yield in such systems requires careful calibration of nutrient delivery and lighting conditions. Recent advances in precision agriculture have facilitated the fine-tuning of these parameters, enabling growers to achieve consistent quality and productivity.  

**2. Nutrient Delivery Systems**  
Hydroponic lettuce production commonly employs nutrient film technique (NFT), deep water culture (DWC), or aeroponic systems. Each method presents distinct challenges in nutrient management, particularly with respect to maintaining optimal electrical conductivity (EC) and pH levels.  
   
**2.1 Recirculating Nutrient Solutions**  
Recirculating systems reduce water consumption and nutrient wastage by continuously cycling the nutrient solution through plant root zones. Studies have shown that maintaining EC between 1.4–1.8 mS cm⁻¹ and pH between 5.8–6.2 supports optimal lettuce growth [2]. Automated dosing systems employing ion-selective sensors can adjust nutrient concentrations in real time, preventing deficiencies or toxicities.  

**2.2 Nutrient Formulation**  
Balanced macro- and micronutrient formulations are critical. Lettuce requires adequate nitrogen for leaf expansion, potassium for turgor maintenance, and calcium for structural integrity. Chelated micronutrients such as iron, manganese, and zinc improve availability in hydroponic solutions, particularly under fluctuating pH conditions. Controlled-release supplementation and frequent monitoring mitigate nutrient imbalances that can predispose plants to physiological disorders like tip burn.  

**3. Artificial Lighting Optimization**  
Light quality, intensity, and photoperiod directly influence lettuce morphology, photosynthetic efficiency, and secondary metabolite accumulation.  

**3.1 Spectral Composition**  
LED technology enables precise spectral tuning to match plant photoreceptor sensitivities. Red light (~660 nm) promotes leaf expansion, while blue light (~450 nm) enhances chlorophyll synthesis and compact growth habit [3]. Ratios of red to blue light between 4:1 and 6:1 have been associated with optimal lettuce biomass production. Supplemental far-red light (~730 nm) can influence shade-avoidance responses, accelerating canopy closure and increasing light interception efficiency.  

**3.2 Light Intensity and Photoperiod**  
Daily light integral (DLI) targets for hydroponic lettuce typically range from 12–17 mol m⁻² d⁻¹. Excessive light intensity can induce photoinhibition, while insufficient levels slow growth and reduce quality. Photoperiods of 14–16 hours have been shown to balance vegetative growth with energy efficiency. Integration of dimmable LED fixtures with environmental control systems allows dynamic adjustment based on plant developmental stage and ambient conditions.  

**4. Pest Reduction Strategies in Controlled Environments**  
While indoor hydroponic systems inherently reduce exposure to soil-borne pathogens and pests, high-density planting and stable microclimates can favor outbreaks of certain insects and fungal diseases. Optimized nutrient and lighting regimes contribute indirectly to pest suppression by promoting vigorous, resilient plants. Additionally, ultraviolet-B (UV-B) supplementation has been observed to induce plant defense responses, reducing the incidence of powdery mildew [4].  

**5. Conclusions**  
Commercial hydroponic lettuce production benefits from integrated optimization of nutrient delivery systems and artificial lighting configurations. Recirculating nutrient solutions with real-time monitoring enhance resource efficiency and plant health, while tailored LED spectra and controlled photoperiods improve growth and quality. These strategies not only maximize yield but also reduce the risk of pest and pathogen outbreaks. Future research should explore the synergistic effects of spectral modulation and nutrient dynamics on secondary metabolite profiles, as well as the economic implications of large-scale system automation.

**Report: Urban Rainwater Runoff and Its Influence on Coastal Erosion Patterns – Mitigation Through Seawalls and Mangrove Restoration**  

---

**Abstract**  
Urban shorelines face increasing pressures from altered hydrological cycles, particularly the intensification of rainwater runoff due to impervious surface expansion. This report examines the relationship between runoff and coastal erosion patterns, with specific attention to metropolitan areas adjacent to tidal zones. It evaluates the efficacy of engineered seawalls and ecological mangrove restoration as complementary mitigation strategies.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
Coastal cities are complex interfaces between terrestrial and marine environments, where urbanization has significantly modified natural water pathways. Rainwater runoff, once absorbed or diffused through vegetation and permeable soils, is now rapidly channeled into storm drains and directly discharged into bays, estuaries, and open coasts. This altered flow regime increases peak discharge rates, delivering sediment, pollutants, and excess freshwater to sensitive coastal systems. The cumulative effect can exacerbate erosion, destabilize shorelines, and degrade habitat quality [1].  

---

**2. Rainwater Runoff and Erosion Dynamics**  
In natural conditions, rainfall infiltrates into soils, replenishes groundwater, and slowly releases into coastal waters. Urban development replaces these surfaces with asphalt, concrete, and rooftops, accelerating runoff velocity and volume. This surge in freshwater flow during storm events can:  

- Dislodge sediment along river mouths and tidal inlets.  
- Alter salinity gradients critical to estuarine ecosystems.  
- Increase hydraulic stress on coastal embankments.  

A notable pattern in urban shorelines is the formation of localized erosion “hot spots” downstream of major stormwater outfalls. These areas often display rapid shoreline retreat, undermining infrastructure and recreational spaces [2].  

---

**3. Seawalls as an Engineered Mitigation Tool**  
Seawalls are vertical or sloped structures built to absorb and deflect wave energy, thereby protecting inland areas from erosion and storm surge. In contexts where rainwater-driven currents exacerbate shoreline loss, seawalls can:  

- Stabilize the immediate coastline by preventing direct scouring.  
- Reduce sediment displacement during combined rainfall and tidal events.  

However, seawalls can also intensify erosion at their base or adjacent unprotected sections, known as “end effect” erosion. Long-term maintenance and integration with drainage systems are essential to minimize such unintended consequences [3].  

---

**4. Mangrove Restoration as a Nature-Based Solution**  
Mangroves, with their dense root systems, act as living barriers against erosion. They dissipate wave energy, trap sediments, and provide critical habitat. Restoration efforts in urban coastal zones involve replanting native mangrove species along degraded shorelines and estuarine fringes.  

Benefits include:  
- Enhanced sediment retention, reducing erosion rates.  
- Filtering of runoff-borne pollutants before they reach open water.  
- Increased resilience to storm surges and tidal fluctuations.  

Mangrove zones also create a buffer that slows rainwater discharge, allowing more gradual mixing with seawater and reducing abrupt hydrological impacts [4].  

---

**5. Integrating Seawalls and Mangrove Restoration**  
The most effective strategies often combine engineered and ecological methods. For example, a seawall can protect critical infrastructure while mangroves seaward of the wall absorb wave and current energy, trap sediments, and provide ecological benefits. This hybrid approach requires careful design to ensure tidal exchange and root growth are not impeded.  

Urban planners can integrate stormwater management with shoreline protection by:  
- Redirecting runoff to vegetated buffer zones before coastal discharge.  
- Designing seawalls with lower crests or permeable sections to allow controlled water exchange.  
- Allocating restoration zones in tandem with public access areas to promote stewardship.  

---

**6. Conclusion**  
Rainwater runoff from urban environments significantly influences coastal erosion patterns, especially in densely developed shoreline regions. Addressing these challenges demands a dual approach: engineered structures such as seawalls to provide immediate defense, and ecological restoration, particularly of mangrove habitats, to foster long-term resilience. By aligning urban stormwater management with coastal protection strategies, cities can reduce erosion, safeguard infrastructure, and enhance ecological integrity.  

---

### What is the difference between biodegradable plastic and compostable plastic? Plastic that is compostable is biodegradable, but not every plastic that is biodegradable is compostable. Whereas biodegradable plastic may be engineered to biodegrade in soil or water, compostable plastic refers to biodegradation into soil conditioning material (i.e., compost) under a certain set of conditions. In order for a plastic to be labeled as commercially “compostable” it must able to be broken down by biological treatment at a commercial or industrial composting facility. Composting utilizes microorganisms, heat and humidity to yield carbon dioxide, water, inorganic compounds, and biomass that is similar in characteristic to the rest of the finished compost product. Decomposition of the plastic must occur at a rate similar to the other elements of the material being composted (within 6 months) and leave no toxic residue that would adversely impact the ability of the finished compost to support plant growth. ASTM Standards D6400 and D6868 outline the specifications that must be met in order to label a plastic as commercially “compostable”. There are currently no ASTM standard test methods in place for evaluating the ability of a plastic to compost in a home environment. ### What are biobased plastics? Biobased plastics are manufactured from plant materials instead of being made from oil or natural gas. Because they are plant based, there is a tendency to assume that this type of plastic must be biodegradable. However, biobased plastics can be designed to be structurally identical to petroleum based plastics, and if designed in this way, they can last in the environment for the same period of time as petroleum based plastic. Just as with petroleum-based plastics, biobased plastic can be engineered to be biodegradable or to be compostable. The ability of biobased plastics to be recycled varies. Some forms of biobased plastic cannot be recycled together with petroleum-based plastics due to chemical structure incompatibility, while other biobased plastics may have compatible chemical structures that allow for recycling together with petroleum-based plastics. In order to determine what waste disposal options are available for a biobased plastic item, it is necessary to read the product’s label as to its compostability and recyclability. ### Which organizations are responsible for creating standards and enforcing correct labeling of biodegradable and compostable plastics? The American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM International) sets definitions and standards, while the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is responsible for enforcement against false or deceptive product labeling. ### If a plastic product is labeled “compostable,” can I add it to my home compost pile? No. Unless the label indicates that the product is okay for home composting, you should not try to compost it at home. Plastic that is labeled as compostable is generally intended to be sent to an industrial or commercial composting facility which has higher temperatures and different breakdown conditions than those found in a typical homeowner’s compost bin. If your community has a residential compost collection program, check with your local government or recycling company to find out if they will accept compostable plastic under this program. ### What if my community doesn’t have a composting recycling pick-up program. Should I dispose of compostable plastic in the plastic recycling pick-up bins? No. Compostable plastics are not intended for recycling and can contaminate and disrupt the recycling stream if intermixed with petroleum-based plastics that are non-compostable. If your community does not have a composting recycling pick-up program that accepts compostable plastic, contact your garbage/recycling company or local government to find out if there are any drop-off locations for your compostable plastic items. ### What is the purpose of plastic bag bans? The Pollution Prevention Act establishes a national objective for environmental protection: “\[T\]hat pollution should be prevented or reduced at the source whenever feasible.” Similarly, the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act sets the order of preference for managing materials as: source reduction, reuse, recycling, and disposal. With these objectives in mind, a number of communities are initiating bans of plastic bags that are intended for single use, such as those commonly provided in grocery stores. The rationale behind the bag bans includes the following: * They are typically made out of petroleum-based plastic and don’t biodegrade when they are disposed of or escape into the environment; * when plastic bags are disposed of on land they may be blown into creeks, lakes, or oceans where they can entangle marine life or the animals may mistakenly eat the plastic bags thinking that they are food; * the light-weight plastic is not easily recyclable; and * the bags are often used only once before being thrown away. The various bag bans differ but typically contain many of the same elements: * Replacement bags typically must be compostable or recyclable. That means that if the replacement bags are made of plastic, the plastic must either be compostable and labeled as such, or the bag must be heavier and thicker such that it won’t interfere with the industrial recycling process, is washable, can carry more weight, and be used multiple times (as many as 125 uses). * Replacement paper bags are typically required to be made of 40% recycled paper and be 100% recyclable. * Many plastic bag bans require retailers to charge a fee per replacement bag which is kept by the retailer. * The purpose of the fee is to both to encourage customers to bring their own reusable bags (minimizing the need to manufacture new bags) and to cover the cost to the retailer of providing bags that are other than single use.

**Creating the Perfect Outdoor Fire Pit: Design Trends and Safety Considerations**  

Outdoor fire pits have evolved far beyond their utilitarian roots, becoming a centerpiece for backyard leisure and social connection. Homeowners are increasingly incorporating fire features into landscape designs, blending functionality with artistic flair. Today’s trends emphasize not only the warmth and ambiance of a flame but also the integration of durable materials, thoughtful layouts, and safety-conscious planning.  

### The Rise of Aesthetic-Focused Fire Pit Design  

A decade ago, many residential fire pits were simple metal bowls or brick circles tucked into a corner of the yard. Modern designs now view the fire pit as an anchor for outdoor living spaces. Circular or square shapes remain popular, but designers are experimenting with geometric forms, multi-tiered structures, and even built-in table-style pits. The visual appeal is heightened by using materials such as hand-cut stone, weathered steel, concrete composites, and ceramic tile. These materials not only withstand the elements but also complement the surrounding landscape architecture.  

Stone fire pits, for example, can be crafted from granite, limestone, or sandstone to blend seamlessly with patios and garden paths. Metal options, often fabricated from corten steel or stainless steel, offer a sleek, contemporary aesthetic and can be customized with intricate cut-out patterns that cast shadow designs when lit.  

### Integrating Seating and Gathering Spaces  

One of the most notable trends is the deliberate integration of seating into the fire pit area. Built-in stone benches, semi-circular wooden seating, or modular outdoor furniture help define the gathering zone and encourage longer, more comfortable visits. The seating arrangement often mirrors the fire pit’s shape, creating a sense of unity and balance. Designers suggest placing seats at a distance that allows for both warmth and safety—typically 3 to 5 feet from the flame source—while ensuring unobstructed views and pathways.  

Some homeowners opt for multi-functional designs where the fire pit doubles as a coffee table when covered, or includes an extended ledge for resting drinks and small plates. This versatility enhances the space’s usability across seasons, even when a fire is not lit.  

### Material Selection for Longevity and Style  

Choosing the right material is about more than aesthetics; it affects durability, maintenance, and overall safety. Stone offers timeless appeal and resilience, with natural variations in color and texture that make each installation unique. Metal fire pits are prized for their clean lines and modern look, but require attention to heat dispersion and potential rust prevention. Composite materials—such as concrete mixed with glass or resin—are gaining traction for their ability to mimic natural stone while offering lighter weight and easier installation.  

In addition, heat-resistant coatings and sealants can protect surfaces from weathering and discoloration, extending the life of the fire pit. Matching the fire pit’s material palette to that of nearby patios, decks, or garden features creates a cohesive outdoor environment.  

### Safety Tips for Backyard Placement  

While design is paramount, safe placement is essential. Fire pits should be located on level ground, away from overhanging branches, fences, or structures, and positioned in areas with good ventilation. Non-combustible surfaces—such as stone pavers or gravel—beneath and around the pit reduce risk.  

For wood-burning models, a spark screen can help contain embers, while gas-fueled designs benefit from automatic shut-off valves. Homeowners should always maintain a clear perimeter around the pit and keep a fire extinguisher or bucket of water nearby during use.  

Lighting and pathways also play a role in safety. Soft, low-voltage lights can guide guests to and from the fire pit area without glare, and defined walkways minimize tripping hazards.  

### Bringing It All Together  

An outdoor fire pit can serve as the heart of backyard gatherings, drawing friends and family together for conversation and relaxation. By embracing current design trends—such as the use of premium materials, integrated seating, and versatile layouts—homeowners can create a space that’s both beautiful and functional. Coupling these design choices with careful attention to placement and safety ensures that the fire pit will remain a cherished feature for years to come.  

Whether rustic stone or modern steel, the right fire pit transforms an outdoor space into a warm, inviting retreat, offering a perfect blend of style and practicality. With thoughtful planning, your backyard can become the ultimate destination for cozy evenings under the stars.

**Tropical Ornamental Plants**  

Tropical ornamental plants encompass a wide array of species cultivated primarily for their vivid flowers, striking foliage, and ability to lend an exotic character to gardens, courtyards, and public landscapes. Many originate from equatorial regions where warm temperatures, high humidity, and abundant rainfall create ideal conditions for lush growth. Their cultivation outside native habitats often requires careful attention to soil composition, irrigation, and microclimate management.  

---

**Propagation Methods**  

Propagation of tropical ornamentals varies according to species and desired growth form. Common techniques include:  

- **Seed propagation**: Frequently used for annual or short-lived perennials such as *Hibiscus rosa-sinensis*. Seeds require warm soil temperatures (25–30°C) and consistent moisture for germination.  
- **Stem cuttings**: Many woody ornamentals, including *Bougainvillea* and *Plumeria*, root readily from semi-hardwood or hardwood cuttings when treated with rooting hormones and kept in a well-drained medium.  
- **Division**: Herbaceous species such as *Heliconia* and *Canna* can be divided at the rhizome or tuber level, ensuring each section contains viable buds.  
- **Layering**: Air layering is particularly effective for certain tropical shrubs and small trees with brittle stems, enabling root formation while still attached to the parent plant.  

Propagation success is influenced by temperature stability, humidity levels, and protection from direct midday sun during the establishment phase.  

---

**Optimal Soil Conditions**  

Tropical ornamentals generally thrive in soils that balance moisture retention with adequate drainage. A loamy texture enriched with organic matter supports robust growth. Key considerations include:  

- **pH range**: Most species prefer slightly acidic to neutral soils (pH 6.0–7.0), though some, such as *Ixora coccinea*, favor more acidic conditions.  
- **Nutrient profile**: Tropical plants often benefit from high potassium and moderate nitrogen to promote flowering without excessive vegetative growth.  
- **Drainage**: Raised beds or amended soils with coarse sand or perlite can prevent waterlogging, a common issue in heavy clay substrates.  
- **Mulching**: Organic mulches regulate soil temperature, suppress weeds, and contribute slow-release nutrients as they decompose.  

In container culture, lightweight potting mixes formulated for tropical species improve root aeration and reduce the risk of fungal diseases.  

---

**Aesthetic Uses in Landscape Design**  

Tropical ornamentals lend themselves to diverse design applications:  

- **Specimen planting**: Large, dramatic species such as *Cordyline fruticosa* or *Alpinia purpurata* serve as focal points in gardens, drawing attention through bold color and form.  
- **Mass planting**: Groupings of *Hibiscus*, *Bougainvillea*, or *Mussaenda* create vibrant borders or hedges, offering seasonal or year-round color.  
- **Mixed borders**: Combining plants with contrasting foliage—such as the finely divided leaves of *Jacaranda mimosifolia* with the broad leaves of *Colocasia esculenta*—adds textural depth.  
- **Container arrangements**: Portable displays of tropical ornamentals allow flexibility in positioning for optimal light exposure and seasonal interest.  
- **Vertical elements**: Vining species like *Thunbergia grandiflora* and climbing *Allamanda cathartica* provide coverage for trellises, pergolas, and walls, integrating living architecture into outdoor spaces.  

Landscape designers often use tropical ornamentals to evoke a sense of lush abundance, combining species with staggered bloom times for continuous display. Careful placement according to light requirements—full sun for *Bougainvillea*, filtered shade for *Anthurium andreanum*—ensures sustained health and ornamental value.  

---

**Maintenance Considerations**  

Routine care includes pruning to maintain form and encourage flowering, periodic fertilization with balanced or bloom-promoting formulas, and monitoring for pests such as aphids, mealybugs, and scale insects. In tropical climates, consistent rainfall may reduce irrigation needs, but supplemental watering during dry spells is essential for species with high moisture demands.  

Deadheading spent blooms in plants like *Hibiscus* prolongs the flowering period, while removing old canes in rhizomatous species such as *Heliconia* stimulates new growth. Seasonal adjustments to shade or wind protection may be required during particularly intense weather events.  

---

**Conclusion**  

Tropical ornamental plants offer exceptional diversity in color, form, and texture, making them indispensable elements in landscape design across warm regions. Successful cultivation depends on understanding each species’ propagation requirements, soil preferences, and maintenance needs. When integrated thoughtfully, these plants can transform spaces into vibrant, enduring displays of botanical richness.

**Report: Advancements in Lightweight Composite Materials for Commercial Aircraft**  

---

**Abstract**  
Over the past two decades, the aerospace industry has increasingly adopted advanced lightweight composite materials in commercial aircraft design and manufacturing. These materials, primarily carbon fiber-reinforced polymers (CFRPs) and hybrid composites, offer significant weight reductions compared to traditional aluminum alloys, directly contributing to improved fuel efficiency and lower operating costs. This report examines recent developments in composite technology, manufacturing processes, and their integration into aircraft structures, with a focus on quantifiable performance benefits and challenges related to large-scale implementation.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
The pursuit of fuel efficiency in commercial aviation is driven by both economic pressures and environmental regulations. Aircraft weight is a critical determinant of fuel consumption, and even incremental reductions can yield substantial savings over an aircraft’s operational life. Composites, particularly CFRPs, have emerged as a transformative material class for primary and secondary aircraft structures. Their high strength-to-weight ratio, corrosion resistance, and ability to be molded into aerodynamically optimized shapes position them as a preferred choice over conventional metals.  

---

**2. Material Properties and Advantages**  
Carbon fiber-reinforced polymers consist of carbon fibers embedded in a polymer matrix, typically epoxy resin. This combination yields tensile strengths up to 4,000 MPa and stiffness values exceeding those of aluminum alloys, while reducing density by approximately 20–30% [1]. Hybrid composites, integrating carbon and glass fibers or thermoplastic matrices, provide tailored performance characteristics for specific applications such as fuselage panels or control surfaces.  

Key advantages include:  
- **Weight Reduction:** CFRPs can reduce airframe weight by 15–20% compared to traditional designs.  
- **Fuel Efficiency Gains:** Lower weight translates to reduced fuel burn, with estimates of 3–5% savings per flight cycle for large aircraft.  
- **Corrosion Resistance:** Composites do not suffer from galvanic corrosion, reducing maintenance requirements.  
- **Design Flexibility:** Complex geometries and integrated structures can be fabricated with fewer joints, improving aerodynamic performance.  

---

**3. Applications in Commercial Aircraft**  
Modern commercial aircraft, such as the Boeing 787 Dreamliner and Airbus A350 XWB, incorporate composites in over 50% of their primary structure by weight. Critical components include:  
- **Fuselage Sections:** Large composite barrel sections replace multiple aluminum panels, reducing assembly complexity.  
- **Wing Structures:** Composite wings allow for increased span and optimized curvature, enhancing lift-to-drag ratios.  
- **Tail Assemblies:** Vertical and horizontal stabilizers benefit from reduced mass and improved fatigue performance.  

---

**4. Manufacturing Innovations**  
Advances in automated fiber placement (AFP) and resin transfer molding (RTM) have improved production efficiency and material consistency. AFP enables precise layering of fibers to achieve desired strength profiles, while RTM offers cost-effective fabrication for medium-size components. Out-of-autoclave curing methods are gaining traction, reducing energy consumption and enabling larger part production without massive autoclave infrastructure.  

---

**5. Performance and Economic Impact**  
Fuel savings from composite integration have direct cost implications. For a long-haul twin-aisle aircraft, a 20% structural weight reduction can save millions of liters of fuel annually, translating into significant operational cost reductions. Additionally, lower maintenance requirements and extended service intervals contribute to reduced lifecycle costs.  

---

**6. Challenges and Future Directions**  
Despite the benefits, several challenges remain:  
- **Material Costs:** CFRPs are more expensive than aluminum alloys, impacting initial acquisition costs.  
- **Repair Complexity:** Composite damage assessment and repair require specialized training and equipment.  
- **Recycling and End-of-Life Management:** Current recycling methods for CFRPs are limited, with ongoing research into reclaiming fibers and resins without degrading performance.  
- **Production Scalability:** High-precision manufacturing processes must meet increasing demand without compromising quality.  

Future research is focusing on bio-based resins, improved recyclability, and hybrid composites that balance cost and performance. Integration of nanomaterials such as graphene into composite matrices is being explored to enhance electrical conductivity and impact resistance.  

---

**7. Conclusion**  
Lightweight composite materials represent a pivotal advancement in commercial aircraft design, offering tangible fuel efficiency gains and weight reductions. Continued innovation in material science, manufacturing technology, and end-of-life solutions will determine the extent to which these materials can be adopted across the aviation industry. As airlines and manufacturers strive to meet stringent environmental and economic targets, composites are poised to play an increasingly central role in shaping the next generation of commercial aircraft.  

---

**References**

[2] Martin, L., et al. (2020). *Innovations in Composite Manufacturing for Large Aircraft Structures*. Aerospace Engineering Review, 28(2), 112–130.

**From Waste to Wonder: Cities Transform Old Landfills into Thriving Green Spaces**  

*By Staff Reporter*  

In a growing number of municipalities across the country, the sight of towering mounds of refuse is giving way to rolling lawns, walking trails, and vibrant community hubs. Decommissioned landfills—once environmental liabilities and eyesores—are being repurposed into public recreation areas through coordinated landscaping, community involvement, and targeted economic investment.  

**A New Chapter for Old Landfills**  
For decades, closed landfill sites were often left fenced off, their potential untapped due to safety concerns and remediation costs. Today, advances in environmental engineering and a shift in urban planning priorities are changing that narrative. Cities such as Riverton, Fairbrook, and Westhaven have recently announced multimillion-dollar projects to cap and rehabilitate old dump sites, integrating them into local green space networks.  

In Riverton, the former East Ridge landfill, closed in the late 1980s, is now the centerpiece of a 65-acre public park. The transformation began with the installation of protective liners and methane capture systems, ensuring the site met stringent environmental safety standards. Landscaping crews then sculpted gentle slopes, planted native grasses and trees, and constructed rain gardens to manage stormwater runoff.  

**Designing for Ecology and Recreation**  
Landscape architects are playing a pivotal role in these conversions, balancing ecological restoration with public usability. In Fairbrook’s Meadowview Park, designers incorporated pollinator-friendly plantings and wetland restoration areas alongside sports fields and playgrounds. Trails wind through replanted woodlands, offering visitors scenic routes that also serve as habitat corridors for local wildlife.  

“By using native species and sustainable design practices, we’re not just creating a park—we’re rebuilding an ecosystem,” said lead landscape architect Dana Hughes. “The goal is to ensure these spaces thrive for generations.”  

**Community Engagement Drives Success**  
Municipal leaders have found that involving residents early in the process fosters a sense of ownership and stewardship. In Westhaven, community workshops allowed locals to weigh in on amenities, from picnic shelters to art installations. Volunteer planting days brought hundreds of residents together, strengthening neighborhood ties while advancing the project’s goals.  

Local schools have also joined in, integrating the park’s development into environmental science curricula. Students participate in monitoring soil health, water quality, and biodiversity, turning the site into a living laboratory.  

**Economic Revitalization Through Green Investment**  
Beyond environmental benefits, landfill reclamation projects are delivering tangible economic returns. New parks attract visitors from surrounding areas, boosting foot traffic for nearby businesses. In Riverton, the East Ridge Park project spurred the opening of several cafes and outdoor gear shops along the adjacent main street.  

Property values in neighborhoods bordering these redeveloped sites have risen, reflecting the appeal of accessible green space. According to a recent municipal report, homes within a half-mile of East Ridge Park appreciated at a rate 12% higher than the city average over the past three years.  

Funding for these projects often comes from a mix of municipal budgets, state environmental grants, and private sponsorships. The Westhaven initiative secured contributions from local corporations seeking to demonstrate corporate social responsibility, further cementing the partnership between public and private sectors.  

**Challenges and Long-Term Stewardship**  
While the transformations are inspiring, they are not without challenges. Ensuring long-term safety requires ongoing monitoring of subsurface conditions, particularly gas emissions and leachate movement. Maintenance budgets must account for specialized infrastructure, such as venting systems and reinforced soil caps.  

Municipalities are addressing these concerns through adaptive management plans. Regular environmental audits, coupled with community-led oversight committees, help identify and address emerging issues before they escalate.  

**A Model for Sustainable Urban Renewal**  
The successful conversion of decommissioned landfills into public parks is becoming a model for sustainable urban renewal. By turning once-blighted areas into ecological and social assets, cities are demonstrating that environmental remediation can go hand-in-hand with economic and cultural revitalization.  

As more municipalities explore these possibilities, residents can look forward to seeing landscapes once defined by waste transformed into spaces of recreation, learning, and community pride—proof that with vision and collaboration, even the most unlikely sites can be reborn as places of beauty and benefit.

Asparagus (Asparagus officinalis) is a perennial crop that can remain productive for 15-20 years or more, making it a valuable crop for many growers. However, due to its perennial nature, asparagus plantings are particularly vulnerable to weed pressure. Weeds can compete with asparagus for water, nutrients, and sunlight, leading to reduced yields and shorter productive lifespans. Weed control is especially critical during the first few years after planting, as young asparagus plants are less competitive and more susceptible to weed-related stress. This article will discuss several weed management options for asparagus, including non-chemical and chemical approaches. ### Non-Chemical Weed Management Non-chemical weed management can be a successful and sustainable approach to weed control in asparagus, though it may require more labor than chemical management options. Some non-chemical strategies include cultivation, mulches, and living mulches / cover crops. #### Mulches Mulches like straw, wood chips, and compost can be very effective at reducing annual weed pressure, preserving soil moisture, and can even suppress perennial weeds like Canada thistle. Mulches should be applied uniformly at a depth of 4-6 inches. Mulches can be applied throughout the planting, or just in between rows to maintain access to the crop. Do not apply mulch directly over the asparagus crown as it can lead to root rot. While mulches can significantly reduce weed pressure, they need to be reapplied every 1-3 years depending on the material used. Additionally, organic mulches can provide habitat for voles, which can damage asparagus crowns by feeding on them. Therefore, if you use mulches, it is important to monitor for vole activity and take appropriate measures if populations become too high. #### Living Mulches / Cover Crops Cover crops, also known as living mulches, are plants that are grown specifically to suppress weeds and improve soil health. In perennial crops like asparagus, cover crops are often planted in between rows to suppress weeds and improve soil health. Common cover crops include rye, oats, clover, and hairy vetch. Some legumes like clover and vetch can fix nitrogen, reducing the need for fertilizer, while grains like rye and oats can add organic matter to the soil. Living mulches can be an excellent way to reduce weeds and improve soil health in established asparagus plantings. However, care must be taken to not allow the living mulch to outcompete the asparagus for water or nutrients. This can be done by mowing or tilling the cover crop at appropriate times. There is also some research being done on using shade-tolerant cover crops in the asparagus row itself, but these are not yet widely recommended.

**Crafting Decorative Handmade Ant Figurines with Non-Toxic Clay and Natural Dyes**  

There is a quiet charm in transforming everyday inspirations into art, and few creatures capture the imagination quite like ants. Their intricate shapes and segmented bodies lend themselves beautifully to miniature sculpture projects. For the home décor enthusiast or art hobbyist, creating ant-shaped figurines can be a satisfying way to fuse creativity with a respect for nature. This guide explores a step-by-step process for crafting these figurines using non-toxic clay and natural dyes—perfect for those who want to produce safe, eco-friendly pieces that can be displayed anywhere in the home.  

---

### Choosing Your Materials  

**Non-toxic clay** is the foundation of this project. Air-dry clays made from natural earth compounds or cornstarch-based blends are ideal, particularly for indoor projects. They are free from harmful chemicals and safe to handle without gloves.  

For coloring, opt for **natural dyes** derived from plants, fruits, and minerals. Common choices include:  
- **Beetroot powder** for reds and pinks  
- **Turmeric powder** for warm yellows  
- **Spirulina powder** for deep greens  
- **Cocoa powder** for rich browns  

These pigments can be mixed into the clay before shaping or applied as surface decoration after the figurine dries.  

---

### Designing the Figurine  

Ants have a distinctive anatomy that can be simplified for artistic effect:  
1. **Head** – small and slightly rounded, with tiny mandible details.  
2. **Thorax** – oval-shaped midsection, slightly smaller than the abdomen.  
3. **Abdomen** – larger rounded section that tapers at the end.  

A typical figurine can be made in a stylized form, with exaggerated proportions for a whimsical look, or kept anatomically accurate for a realistic miniature.  

Sketching the design beforehand helps with proportion and placement of limbs.  

---

### Step-by-Step Crafting Process  

**Step 1: Prepare the Clay**  
If using powdered natural dyes, knead the pigment thoroughly into the clay until evenly distributed. This prevents streaking and ensures consistent color.  

**Step 2: Form the Segments**  
Roll three clay balls of varying sizes for the head, thorax, and abdomen. Use gentle pressure to shape them into slightly elongated ovals.  

**Step 3: Join the Body Parts**  
Lightly score the connecting surfaces with a craft knife or toothpick, then press them together. For added stability, insert a small piece of toothpick or wire between sections before pressing.  

**Step 4: Add Details**  
Use a fine sculpting tool or needle to etch antennae grooves, leg joints, and mandible shapes. For whimsical designs, consider curling the antennae or elongating the legs for a playful effect.  

**Step 5: Drying**  
Place the figurines on a parchment-lined tray and allow them to air dry completely. Depending on clay thickness, drying can take 24–48 hours.  

**Step 6: Surface Decoration**  
Once dry, apply a thin wash of natural dye mixed with water for additional shading. A soft brush works best to avoid streaks.  

---

### Finishing Touches  

For a polished look, you can seal the figurines with a non-toxic, plant-based varnish. This enhances color vibrancy and protects against moisture. Beeswax polish is another gentle alternative that adds a warm sheen without synthetic chemicals.  

If you plan to display the figurines in a communal space like a kitchen or living room, consider arranging them on a small wooden tray or mounting them in a shadow box frame. Grouping several ants together can create a dynamic composition that draws the eye.  

---

### Creative Variations  

- **Miniature Scenes**: Combine ant figurines with clay leaves, twigs, or pebbles to create a diorama.  
- **Themed Colors**: Experiment with unusual hues—such as deep indigo from butterfly pea flowers—for a surreal, artistic interpretation.  
- **Jewelry Adaptations**: Smaller figurines can be turned into brooches, pendants, or charm beads by embedding loops before drying.  

---

### Caring for Your Figurines  

Non-toxic clay pieces are generally durable, but they benefit from gentle handling. Avoid prolonged exposure to direct sunlight, which can fade natural dyes over time. Dust occasionally with a soft cloth to keep the surface clean.  

---

By working with safe, natural materials, you can create decorative ant figurines that are both charming and environmentally conscious. Whether displayed as part of a nature-inspired collection or given as handmade gifts, these little sculptures carry a unique personality and a story of mindful craftsmanship. The process itself—slow, deliberate, and creative—becomes part of the enjoyment, turning a simple idea into a lasting piece of art.

**Energize Your Life: Exercises and Habits to Boost Stamina and Wellness**  

In today’s fast-paced world, maintaining energy and stamina throughout the day can feel like a constant challenge. Whether you’re balancing work, family, and hobbies or simply aiming to feel more vibrant, combining targeted exercise routines with smart dietary choices can dramatically improve your vitality. Below, we’ll explore three powerful approaches—yoga, high-intensity interval training (HIIT), and nutritional strategies—designed to help you build lasting stamina and enhance overall wellness.  

---

### **Yoga for Sustained Energy and Mind-Body Balance**  

Yoga is more than just stretching—it’s a holistic practice that nurtures both mental clarity and physical endurance. Certain sequences are especially effective for boosting energy:  

- **Sun Salutations (Surya Namaskar):** This flowing sequence warms the body, increases circulation, and awakens your muscles. Performing 5–10 rounds in the morning can help set a vibrant tone for the day.  
- **Warrior Series (Virabhadrasana I, II, III):** These poses strengthen the legs, hips, and core while improving focus and stability. Holding each pose for 20–30 seconds challenges stamina and builds resilience.  
- **Backbends (Bridge Pose, Camel Pose):** Gentle backbends open the chest, improve lung capacity, and stimulate the nervous system, helping you feel more alert.  

Consistency is key—aim for a 20–30 minute yoga session three to five times a week. Over time, you’ll notice greater flexibility, improved posture, and a calmer mind, all of which contribute to sustained energy levels.  

---

### **High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) for Maximum Endurance**  

While yoga builds steady, controlled energy, HIIT is designed to push your stamina to new heights in a short period of time. HIIT involves alternating between short bursts of intense activity and brief recovery periods. This method improves cardiovascular health, increases metabolic rate, and trains your body to recover faster between exertions.  

A sample 15-minute HIIT workout could look like this:  

1. **Jump Squats** – 30 seconds of explosive movement  
2. **Rest** – 15 seconds  
3. **Mountain Climbers** – 30 seconds  
4. **Rest** – 15 seconds  
5. **Burpees** – 30 seconds  
6. **Rest** – 15 seconds  
*(Repeat the circuit 3–4 times)*  

The beauty of HIIT is its adaptability—you can tailor exercises to your fitness level and available space. Just two to three HIIT sessions per week can yield noticeable improvements in endurance within a month.  

---

### **Dietary Tips for All-Day Vitality**  

Energy isn’t just built in the gym or on the yoga mat—it’s also fueled by what you put on your plate. Supporting your exercise routine with nutrient-rich foods ensures your body has the resources it needs for stamina and recovery.  

- **Prioritize Complex Carbohydrates:** Whole grains, legumes, and vegetables provide a steady release of glucose, keeping energy levels stable.  
- **Include Lean Proteins:** Eggs, fish, poultry, tofu, and beans help repair muscle tissue and support long-term strength.  
- **Stay Hydrated:** Even mild dehydration can sap energy—aim for at least 2 liters of water daily, adjusting for activity and climate.  
- **Healthy Fats for Endurance:** Avocados, nuts, seeds, and olive oil help regulate hormone function and maintain satiety.  
- **Time Your Meals Wisely:** Eating a balanced breakfast and smaller, frequent meals can prevent energy crashes.  

Pairing these dietary habits with your exercise regimen creates a synergistic effect: your workouts become more effective, and your daily energy feels more consistent.  

---

### **Putting It All Together**  

The most effective way to cultivate lasting stamina is to blend physical activity with mindful nutrition. Yoga offers grounding, flexibility, and gentle energy enhancement, while HIIT builds cardiovascular capacity and resilience. A balanced diet supports both, ensuring your body has the fuel it needs to perform and recover.  

By dedicating time each week to these practices, you’ll not only improve your physical endurance but also strengthen mental focus and emotional well-being. Over time, the combination of mindful movement, strategic intensity, and clean nutrition can transform your daily life—helping you greet each day with vitality, clarity, and a renewed sense of purpose.  

---

**Action Step:** Choose one yoga sequence and one HIIT workout to integrate into your weekly routine, and pair them with three dietary changes from the list above. Track your energy levels for a month—you may be surprised at how quickly your stamina and wellness improve.

Dengue is a mosquito-borne, acute viral syndrome caused by any of the four serotypes of dengue virus.[1] In 2019, the World Health Organization designated dengue as one of the top 10 global health threats.[2] An estimated 50 million to 100 million symptomatic cases occur globally each year.[3,4] Dengue epidemics occur annually or at multiyear intervals, and the surge in case numbers places considerable pressure on health services.[5] _Aedes aegypti_ mosquitoes are the primary vectors of dengue. Efforts to control _A. aegypti_ populations with the use of insecticides or environmental management methods have not been effective in controlling dengue as a public health problem in most countries.[6] Few randomized trials of _A. aegypti_–control methods have been conducted, and none have used the end point of virologically confirmed dengue (VCD).[7] A trial of community mobilization to reduce the _A. aegypti_ population in Nicaragua and Mexico showed modest efficacy (29.5%) against dengue seroconversion in the saliva of residents.[8] _Wolbachia pipientis_ — a common, maternally inherited, obligate intracellular type of bacteria — infects many species of insects but does not occur naturally in _A. aegypti_.[9] Stable transinfection of _A. aegypti_ with some strains of wolbachia confers resistance to disseminated infection by DENV and other arboviruses.[10-13] Thus, the introgression of “virus-blocking” strains of wolbachia into field populations of _A. aegypti_ is an emerging dengue-control method.[14-17] The approach involves regular releases of wolbachia-infected mosquitoes into a wild mosquito population over a period of several months. Wolbachia facilitates its own population introgression by manipulating reproductive outcomes between wild-type and wolbachia-infected mosquitoes: the only viable mating outcomes are those in which the progeny are infected with wolbachia.[13] Here, we report the results of a cluster-randomized trial that assessed the efficacy of deployments of _A. aegypti_ mosquitoes infected with the _w_ Mel strain of wolbachia in reducing the incidence of VCD in Yogyakarta, Indonesia. The trial builds on earlier entomologic and epidemiologic pilot studies in this geographic setting.[14,18,19] ## Discussion Establishment of _w_ Mel in _A. aegypti_ mosquitoes in Yogyakarta reduced the incidence of symptomatic VCD cases by 77% among residents 3 to 45 years of age. It is reassuring that protective efficacy was observed against all four DENV serotypes and with the greatest confidence observed against DENV-2 and DENV-4, since these were the most prevalent serotypes. The protective efficacy in preventing hospitalization with VCD, a pragmatic proxy of clinical severity, was 86%. In 11 of the 12 intervention clusters, the proportion of participants with VCD in each cluster was lower than that in control clusters, which shows consistent biologic replication of the intervention effect. The conceptual underpinnings of the test-negative design used in this trial, and the statistical framework for population inference, have been described previously.[23] Acute undifferentiated fever for a duration of 1 to 4 days was set as the clinical basis for participant eligibility to avoid selection bias at the point of recruitment and to enable virologic detection of dengue cases. Trial procedures, such as the concealment from research staff of the wolbachia exposure status of the participants, were designed to prevent bias in follow-up, laboratory testing, and outcome classification. The mosquito releases in the intervention clusters were delivered openly (not placebo controlled) for several months in each cluster during 2017. There was no evidence that this changed the health care–seeking behavior of community members in subsequent years, because similar numbers of participants who met the eligibility criteria were enrolled from the intervention and the control clusters. Populations of _w_ Mel-infected mosquitoes were not static, and spatially heterogenous _w_ Mel contamination was measured at the edges of control clusters in year 2 of the trial. Nonetheless, the efficacy estimates from per-protocol analyses, which accounted for individual participants’ recent exposure to _w_ Mel through changes in cluster-level _w_ Mel prevalence or human movement, did not exceed those in the intention-to-treat analysis. We plan more nuanced exploratory analyses outside the scope of the current protocol to explore the fine spatial and temporal connections between _w_ Mel prevalence and the risk of VCD. The efficacy results reported here are consistent with a body of laboratory and field observations. Predictions from an ensemble of mathematical models have suggested that the reduced infectiousness observed in _w_ Mel-infected _A. aegypti_ could be sufficient to reduce the basic reproductive number to below 1 in many settings in which dengue is endemic, which could result in local elimination of disease.[3,25,26] Previous nonrandomized field studies in Australia[16,17] and Indonesia[14] provided evidence of large epidemiologic effects after _w_ Mel was introgressed. A quasi-experimental study of _w_ Mel deployments showed that the incidence of hospitalization with dengue hemorrhagic fever was 76% lower in seven urban villages on the northwestern border of Yogyakarta than in three control villages on the southeastern border of the city during the 30 months after mosquito deployment.[14] Together with the results of the trial reported here, these data suggest that when _w_ Mel is established at high prevalence in local _A. aegypti_ populations, reductions in the incidence of dengue follow. Another wolbachia strain, _w_ AlbB, also has pathogen-blocking properties and can be introgressed into _A. aegypti_ field populations.[15] This suggests the possibility of a portfolio of wolbachia strains, each with different strengths and weaknesses, for application as public health interventions in areas in which dengue is endemic. Stable _w_ Mel transinfection imparts a viral-resistant state in _A. aegypti_ mosquitoes that attenuates superinfection by several medically important flaviviruses and alphaviruses. Multiple mechanisms have been proposed to explain this phenotype, including wolbachia-induced triggering of innate immune effectors[27,28] and changes in intracellular cholesterol transport.[29] DENV could plausibly evolve resistance to _w_ Mel; however, the requirement for alternating infection of human and mosquito hosts, together with what appears to be a complex mode of action, could be a constraint to the adaptive emergence of resistant virus populations. Future research should survey arbovirus populations for signals of wolbachia-associated selective pressure. The approach of _w_ Mel introgression represents a novel product class for the control of dengue.[30] An attractive aspect of this strategy is that it is maintained in the mosquito population and does not need reapplication.[31] Future trials should explore the multivalency of the intervention, since laboratory studies[12,32–35] suggest _w_ Mel could also attenuate transmission of Zika, chikungunya, yellow fever, and Mayaro viruses by _A. aegypti._

Bokashi buckets layer food waste - _including_ meat, bones, and dairy - into a sealed bucket to ferment. The fermented waste then needs to be mixed into a large tub of soil indoors, stirred into a compost pile, or buried in garden soil outdoors to finish decomposing. For a quick introduction, watch the SWRC's 1-minute video Bokashi Composting in 60 Seconds - Make sure your bokashi bucket has either a false bottom or 2-3" of dry sawdust in the bottom to absorb any extra liquid from the fermentation process. - Add food waste (vegetable and fruit scraps, grain-based products, coffee and tea waste, eggshells, meat, bones, dairy, or cooked food) to the bucket in 1" layers. If possible, chop bulky food waste into 2-3" pieces before adding so they can be packed more tightly in the pail. - Sprinkle 1-2 tablespoons (a small handful) of bokashi bran over the food waste. - If you have more food waste to add, repeat the 1" layering and sprinkling of bran. - Place a round item that fits fairly snugly into the bucket, such as a plate, on top of the food waste and press down firmly. This helps expel as much air as possible. _Optional:_ Place a rock or brick on top of the plate to compress the food waste further. - Keep the lid of the bucket closed tightly whenever you are not adding food waste. - If your style of bokashi bucket has a spigot in the bottom for excess liquid, check if there is liquid built up every few days. The tapped liquid makes a good drain cleaner. - White mold should start to grow on the contents within a few days. This mold is not dangerous and means the process is working. The food waste will also develop a sour, beery smell that should only be detectable when the bucket is opened. - When the bucket is full, close it tightly and set it aside to ferment for a minimum of 2 weeks. If it is more convenient, it can also be stored this way for several months. Begin a different bokashi bucket at this time. - Finished buckets eventually need to be emptied into a large tub of soil indoors, stirred into a compost pile, or buried in garden soil outdoors. - If you are using the indoor method, put several inches of garden soil into the bottom of a large tub. (Do not use sterile potting soil for this.) Pour in the contents of your bucket and blend it thoroughly with this soil. Cover with several more inches of soil and leave the tub for 2 weeks. After 2 weeks, you can begin checking how decomposition is going. After 6 weeks, the fermented waste should be totally dissolved. - If you are using an outdoor compost pile, simply pour in the contents of your bucket and stir them in to the previous material. - If you are using an outdoor garden space, dig a hole or trench at least a few inches away from the nearest plants. Pour in the contents of your bucket and blend it with the soil. Cover with several more inches of soil. This area will be temporarily too acidic for planting, but safe after 6-8 weeks. ### What composting style do they fit? Bokashi buckets require a some knowledge but little work to maintain, so they work well for both hands-off and hands-on composters. They work especially well for composters that have occasional access to an outdoor garden or compost space to empty the finished buckets. ### What space does it need? Bokashi buckets need indoor space. The finished buckets also need to be emptied a few times a year into a large tub of soil indoors, an outdoor garden, or an outdoor compost pile. ### How do they work? Bokashi buckets use a mix of lactobacteria, phytobacteria, and yeast (added using inoculated bran) to ferment food waste in an anaerobic environment. While this doesn't change the appearance of the food waste significantly, it alters it dramatically at a cellular level. The food waste is now much easier for regular decomposition microbes to break down. When the fermented waste is added to a tub of soil, outdoor compost, or buried in a garden, decomposition microbes from the environment rapidly colonize the material and dissolve it completely in 2-6 weeks. ### Can you use it all year? Bokashi buckets are an indoor system and can be used all year. During the winter finished buckets can be mixed into a large tub of soil indoors, stored up until spring, or dumped into an outdoor compost bin.
