#### **WHAT IS DBH?** DBH is not a fan convector and is certainly not an electric radiator. The DBH upgrade set is a booster that was specially developed for Jaga Low-H2O radiators to increase heating capacity and enable low energy consumption cooling. As radiators with DBH can achieve such high outputs, it makes it possible to greatly reduce the water flow temperature of your heating system to optimise the performance when used with renewable energy technology. Therefore, you can easily switch from a high flow temperature gas boiler (typically operating at 75/65°C) to a low flow temperature heat pump (typically operating at 45/35°C). The DBH set is made up of small electric activators which, when placed inside a Low-H2O radiator, significantly boost output. The technology is an enhanced version of Jaga’s former Dynamic Boost Effect (DBE), a well-known and trusted technology widely used across the UK and the world. But DBH has the added benefit of providing low cost, environmentally friendly light cooling (non-condensing) when used with a reverse cycle heat pump providing cooled water. Watch this short video to learn more about how DBH works with our best-selling Strada. #### **CAN I FIT DBH TO MY STEEL PANEL RADIATOR?** Regular steel panel radiators are not suitable for a DBH upgrade. DBH is specially designed to be fitted inside a Jaga Low-H2O radiator. If you are moving from a high flow temperature boiler to a low flow temperature heat pump, you will likely have to increase the size of your steel panel radiators by two to three times that of the original. By using Low-H2O with DBH, you can replace your steel panel rads for ones of equivalent size thanks to the powerful heat outputs it can provide at low flow temperatures. #### **WHICH SIZE DBH DO I NEED?** Almost all Jaga Low-H2O radiators can be equipped with the **DBH upgrade set**, including **Strada**, **Tempo**, **Guardian**, **Maxi 2020**. It simply sits on top of the heat exchanger inside the unit to increase the airflow, therefore increasing the output. It’s important to note that the height of the radiator does not affect the output DBH provides. DBH can be fitted inside a radiator as small as 350mm H x 500mm L. The output of the 350mm high Low-H2O Hybrid radiator will be the same as the 950mm high of the same length. This makes it a great option where wall space is limited. DBH comes in two widths, each with various lengths to match the radiator it’s being fitted to. ### DBH Unit 10 Slightly narrower & suitable for Type 10 or Type 11 radiator (115mm depth) ### DBH Unit 15 Slightly wider & suitable for Type 15, 16, 20 oe 21 radiator (165mm-215mm depth) Our team can help you select the right DBH units for your radiators, so you don’t need to worry. #### **DOES DBH USE A LOT OF ELECTRICITY?** In operation, the electricity consumption is on average no more than 7 Watts/metre. The annual consumption is negligible and is more than compensated by the energy efficiency of the Low-H2O technology in the radiator. The power of the DBH unit remains the same regardless of radiator height but does increase as the radiator length increases. For example, a small 350mm H x 500mm L Strada Hybrid Type 11 will use 5.1 Watts of power, and our longest at the same height and type at 2800mm L will use 31.4 Watts. **Here are some typical examples of the daily cost of running DBH:** Living Room - Has a large Strada Hybrid 1600mm long - This would contain 2 x DBH.10F07 (DBH 10 units with 7 thermal activators) - Electricity consumption = 0.12kWh per day - Electricity cost = **£0.02 per day** @ 20p/kWh Bedroom - Has a mid-size Strada Hybrid 1000mm long - This would contain 1 x DBH.10F08 (DBH 10 unit with 8 thermal activators) - Electricity consumption = 0.08kWh per day - Electricity cost = **£0.02 per day** @ 20p/kWh The above calculations are based on the below assumptions: - The unit is on and running in comfort mode (speed 2) for 3 hours in the morning and 4.5 hours in the evening. - The unit is on standby for 9 hours overnight and 7.5 hours during the day. - Boost mode (speed 3) is operated in 15 min intervals totalling 2 hours during the on period. - The electricity cost is 20p/kWh. As a comparison, we can look at the cost of running a TV. Based on a typical 55” LED TV, energy efficiency rating G, in use approx. 2-3 hrs per day, the total electricity cost based on 20p/kWh works out to be £0.06 per day. So running DBH for a typical 7.5 hours per day is a lot cheaper than watching 2-3 hours of TV! #### **IS DBH NOISY?** It’s important to note, that a Low-H2O Hybrid radiator can provide heat naturally without the DBH operating. In this case, it is completely silent. When the D BH is switched on and the fans are running, the unit operates at a very low noise level. DBH has three different fan speeds you can select from to achieve desired temperatures. The lower the fan speed, the quieter it is. 1. Bedroom mode (speed 1) – max. 26 dB(A) 2. Comfort mode (speed 2) – max. 30 dB(A) 3. Boost mode (speed 3) – 42-47.8 dB(A) DBH is selected in comfort mode. This guarantees a quiet operation at a maximum of 30 dB(A). Speed 1 is an extremely quiet bedroom setting with a maximum of 26 dB(A). Speed 3 provides a maximum boost with the very high output serving primarily to heat up and cool down a room as quickly as possible, so is only used for 15-minute periods. In this mode, the noise level is between 42 and 47.8dB(A). The sound power of the DBH is measured in accordance with ISO 3741:2010. The sound power can be described as the cause of the noise. And the sound pressure, the effect of the noise, i.e., what you hear. That’s why we publish sound pressure in our technical information tables. In standard comfort mode, the noise levels of the DBH remains the same regardless of the size of the radiator. For example, a small 350mm H x 500mm L Strada Hybrid will operate at a maximum of 30 dB(A), as will a larger 650mm H x 2800mm L Strada Hybrid. When using the temporary 15-minute Boost mode, this does vary slightly based on the length of the unit. For example, a 350mm H x 500mm L Strada Hybrid Type 11 in boost mode will operate at 38.8 dB(A), and a larger 650mm H x 2800mm L Strada Hybrid Type 11 in boost mode will operate at 47.8 dB(A).

**The Quiet Revolution: Scandinavian Minimalism in 1990s Urban Apartments**  

In the shifting landscape of home interior design, the 1990s marked a subtle yet significant turn toward simplicity, functionality, and light-filled spaces. Nowhere was this more evident than in the embrace of Scandinavian minimalism, a design ethos that quietly but profoundly influenced furniture styles in urban apartments across Europe, North America, and beyond.  

**Historical Context**  
By the late 1980s, many city dwellers had grown weary of the ornate, heavily upholstered furniture and dense color schemes that dominated earlier decades. The cultural climate was changing—globalization brought more exposure to international aesthetics, and urban living spaces were becoming smaller as city populations expanded. In this context, Scandinavian minimalism offered a refreshing alternative: a design philosophy rooted in clean lines, natural materials, and a restrained yet warm color palette.  

Scandinavian design had been evolving since the mid-20th century, shaped by Nordic traditions and the practical needs of living in regions with long, dark winters. The emphasis on maximizing light, using pale woods, and creating uncluttered interiors resonated with urban apartment dwellers seeking both style and efficiency. By the 1990s, these principles were no longer confined to Nordic countries—they were being adapted and reinterpreted in cities from London to New York.  

**Furniture Styles and Material Choices**  
In urban apartments of the era, furniture inspired by Scandinavian minimalism tended toward streamlined silhouettes, often featuring tapered legs, smooth surfaces, and understated detailing. Sofas were low-profile, designed to fit neatly into modest living rooms. Dining tables, frequently crafted from pale birch or ash, were compact yet sturdy, reflecting a focus on durability without excess ornamentation.  

The choice of materials reinforced the minimalist aesthetic. Light-colored woods, sometimes left untreated or finished with a matte sealant, became a hallmark of the style. Metal accents—slender steel frames or brushed aluminum hardware—were used sparingly, often to provide structural integrity without visually weighing down the piece. Upholstery favored neutral fabrics such as linen or cotton, with occasional splashes of muted blues or soft grays.  

**Color Palettes and Emotional Tone**  
Color played a central role in translating Scandinavian minimalism to urban interiors. The 1990s saw a move toward pale, airy tones: white walls to reflect available light, soft beiges to create warmth, and cool grays to add depth without heaviness. Accents were typically subdued—pastel greens, dusty blues, and the occasional terracotta or ochre for contrast.  

This palette was more than an aesthetic choice; it was a response to the realities of urban living. Small apartments benefited from the illusion of spaciousness that lighter colors provided, while the calm, understated hues offered a visual respite from the sensory overload of city life. The emphasis on light and openness also mirrored broader cultural shifts toward wellness and mindful living.  

**Spatial Layout and Functionality**  
Scandinavian minimalism influenced not only the look of furniture but also the way spaces were arranged. In 1990s urban apartments, layouts began to prioritize openness and flow. Furniture was positioned to maximize usable space, often leaving clear sightlines between rooms. Multipurpose pieces—such as extendable dining tables or daybeds—were common, reflecting the need for adaptability in compact environments.  

Storage solutions were discreet, integrated into furniture or built into walls, helping maintain the uncluttered aesthetic. Shelving units were open yet orderly, allowing personal items to be displayed without overwhelming the space. The overall effect was one of intentionality: each piece served a purpose, and nothing was included without consideration.  

**Cultural Impact and Legacy**  
The influence of Scandinavian minimalism in the 1990s extended beyond aesthetics. It encouraged a mindset that valued quality over quantity, timelessness over trend-chasing. Urban dwellers who adopted this style often found themselves curating their possessions more carefully, investing in furniture designed to last rather than to be replaced frequently.  

This approach has had lasting effects on contemporary design. Many principles from the 1990s—such as the integration of natural materials, the prioritization of light, and the commitment to functional beauty—remain relevant in today’s urban interiors. The minimalist ethos continues to inspire new generations, adapting to changing lifestyles while holding onto its core ideals.  

In retrospect, the 1990s can be seen as a pivotal decade in the globalization of Scandinavian minimalism. It was a time when the style’s gentle restraint and human-centered design found fertile ground in cities worldwide, subtly reshaping the way people thought about their homes. Through its careful balance of form and function, it offered a vision of urban living that was both practical and profoundly serene—a vision that endures in countless apartments to this day.

**Report: Environmental Impact of Disposing Industrial Cooking Oils from Large-Scale Restaurant Chains**  

---

**Abstract**  
The disposal of industrial cooking oils, particularly from large-scale restaurant chains, presents significant environmental challenges. This report examines the current waste management policies and recycling regulations governing the handling of used cooking oils, outlines the environmental risks associated with improper disposal, and evaluates emerging best practices in oil recovery and reuse.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
Industrial cooking oils are an integral component of the food service sector, used extensively in frying, baking, and other culinary processes. Large-scale restaurant chains generate considerable quantities of waste oil, often amounting to hundreds of liters per location each week. Without adequate management, the disposal of these oils can cause soil contamination, waterway pollution, and strain on municipal wastewater treatment systems. This report focuses on the regulatory frameworks and environmental considerations shaping current disposal and recycling practices within this sector.  

---

**2. Environmental Risks of Improper Disposal**  
When waste cooking oil is discharged into sewage systems or landfills without treatment, it can solidify and obstruct pipelines, leading to costly maintenance and potential public health hazards. Oil entering waterways forms surface films that reduce oxygen transfer, harming aquatic life. Furthermore, anaerobic decomposition of oils can release methane, a potent greenhouse gas, contributing to climate change. The cumulative impact from large-scale chains, operating hundreds or thousands of outlets, magnifies these risks significantly.  

---

**3. Current Waste Management Policies**  
Many jurisdictions have enacted regulations requiring the collection and proper disposal of used cooking oils. In the United States, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and local municipal codes mandate that food service establishments use licensed grease haulers and maintain records of oil disposal [1]. In the European Union, the Waste Framework Directive (Directive 2008/98/EC) obliges businesses to apply waste hierarchy principles, prioritizing prevention, reuse, and recycling over disposal. Compliance often involves installing grease traps, contracting with certified recyclers, and avoiding direct discharge into public sewers.  

---

**4. Recycling and Reuse Regulations**  
Recycling used cooking oil is increasingly recognized as a viable waste-to-resource pathway. Regulations typically define permissible recycling streams, including:  
- **Biodiesel production**: Waste oil can be processed into biodiesel, reducing reliance on petroleum fuels and lowering net carbon emissions.  
- **Animal feed additives**: After rigorous filtration and testing, certain oils may be incorporated into livestock feed, subject to food safety laws.  
- **Industrial lubricants**: Re-refined oils can serve as lubricants in manufacturing processes.  

In the United States, the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) provides incentives for biodiesel producers using waste oils. Similarly, EU member states offer tax benefits or subsidies for businesses participating in certified oil recycling programs.  

---

**5. Case Studies in Best Practices**  
Several large chains have implemented closed-loop oil recycling systems. For instance, McDonald’s UK collects used cooking oil from all outlets and converts it into biodiesel to fuel delivery trucks, reducing both waste and transportation emissions. Another example is a North American chain partnering with regional recyclers to produce bio-based lubricants for agricultural machinery. These initiatives demonstrate how compliance with regulations can align with corporate sustainability goals.  

---

**6. Challenges and Future Directions**  
Despite regulatory progress, challenges remain. Illegal dumping persists in regions with weak enforcement, and fluctuating market prices for recycled oil products can undermine program viability. Additionally, contamination from cleaning agents or food waste can limit the suitability of oil for certain recycling applications. Future policy directions may include stricter enforcement, expanded public-private partnerships, and incentives for technological innovation in oil purification and conversion.  

---

**7. Conclusion**  
The environmental impact of disposing industrial cooking oils from large-scale restaurant chains is substantial, but manageable through robust waste management policies and effective recycling regulations. By prioritizing responsible collection, encouraging recycling into biodiesel or other products, and supporting industry-wide best practices, governments and businesses can mitigate pollution risks and contribute to broader sustainability objectives.  

---

[2] European Commission. “Directive 2008/98/EC on Waste (Waste Framework Directive).” Official Journal of the European Union, 2008.

**Smart Lawn Care: Choosing the Best Autonomous Robotic Mower for Your Backyard**  

Maintaining a lush, evenly trimmed lawn can be a time-consuming chore, particularly for homeowners who value a tidy backyard but have limited time to devote to yard work. In recent years, autonomous robotic lawn mowers have emerged as a practical, eco-friendly solution that blends convenience with cutting-edge technology. This article explores how to select the right model for residential use, with emphasis on navigation capabilities and battery efficiency—two factors that make the difference between a mediocre mower and a truly smart investment.  

---

### The Rise of Autonomous Lawn Mowing  

Robotic lawn mowers have evolved dramatically since their early iterations. Modern units can map complex yard layouts, negotiate uneven terrain, and operate quietly without disrupting household activities or neighbors. Their popularity stems from two core advantages: automation and sustainability. Unlike traditional gas-powered models, these mowers run on rechargeable batteries, reducing emissions and noise pollution while cutting operational costs over time.  

---

### Navigation Systems: Precision Meets Efficiency  

A mower’s navigation system is the heart of its performance. Advanced models use GPS-assisted mapping, boundary wire sensors, and sometimes camera-based vision to create a virtual map of your backyard. This allows them to optimize cutting patterns, avoid obstacles, and ensure no patch of grass is left untouched.  

For yards with irregular shapes, or those dotted with flower beds, trees, and pathways, a mower with adaptive route planning is crucial. Look for features such as:  

- **Multi-zone programming**: The ability to designate and schedule mowing in different sections of the yard.  
- **Dynamic obstacle detection**: Sensors that allow the mower to adjust course instantly when encountering pets, toys, or unexpected objects.  
- **Return-to-base functionality**: Automatic docking for charging when the battery runs low, ensuring uninterrupted operation.  

These navigation enhancements not only improve the quality of the cut but also reduce the time the mower spends wandering aimlessly, conserving battery life.  

---

### Battery Life and Energy Efficiency  

Battery capacity defines how long a robotic mower can operate before needing a recharge. High-quality lithium-ion batteries are the standard, offering longer runtimes and quicker charging compared to older battery types.  

Key considerations include:  

- **Runtime per charge**: For medium-sized residential yards, aim for at least 60–90 minutes of continuous operation. Larger properties may require models with extended runtimes or swappable battery packs.  
- **Charging speed**: Faster charging minimizes downtime, allowing the mower to resume work promptly.  
- **Smart energy management**: Some mowers adjust cutting speed or blade height based on grass density, conserving power while maintaining performance.  

Energy efficiency isn’t just about battery specs—it’s also about how intelligently the mower uses its stored energy. Models that adapt to lawn conditions and optimize their mowing schedule can significantly reduce electricity consumption over time.  

---

### Durability and Weather Resistance  

Outdoor equipment must endure changing weather conditions. A robust mower should have a weatherproof chassis, sealed electronics, and corrosion-resistant blades. Many high-end models include rain sensors, pausing operation during wet conditions to protect both the mower and the lawn.  

---

### Connectivity and Smart Features  

Integration with mobile apps allows homeowners to monitor and control their mower remotely. Common functions include:  

- Scheduling mowing sessions from a smartphone.  
- Receiving notifications about maintenance needs or obstacle encounters.  
- Tracking performance metrics, such as area covered and battery health.  

Some models even integrate with smart home ecosystems, enabling voice commands or synchronization with other automated outdoor devices.  

---

### Making the Right Choice  

When selecting an autonomous robotic mower, balance your priorities: accurate navigation for thorough coverage, energy-efficient batteries for sustained operation, durable construction for outdoor resilience, and smart connectivity for convenience. By focusing on these aspects, you can ensure your backyard remains neatly trimmed with minimal effort and maximum efficiency.  

---

**Conclusion**  

Autonomous robotic lawn mowers represent a fusion of technological innovation and sustainable landscaping. With advanced navigation systems ensuring precise coverage and energy-efficient batteries driving eco-friendly performance, they offer a reliable and modern approach to lawn care. Investing in a model that matches your yard’s unique characteristics will not only keep your grass in top shape but also free up valuable time for other pursuits.

**Crafting with Foam Pool Noodles: Creative DIY Protective Sleeves for Your Home Décor and Holiday Ornaments**  

Foam pool noodles are a staple of summertime fun, but their versatility extends far beyond the swimming pool. With their light weight, flexibility, and shock-absorbing properties, these colorful cylinders can be transformed into practical, beautiful, and protective solutions for your home. One particularly useful application is crafting custom sleeves to safeguard delicate décor pieces and holiday ornaments.  

### Why Foam Pool Noodles Make Excellent Protective Material  

Pool noodles are made from polyethylene foam, which is soft yet sturdy enough to absorb bumps and prevent scratches. They can be easily cut, shaped, and adapted to fit objects of varying sizes. Unlike hard cases or boxes, foam sleeves are lightweight, reducing strain when storing or transporting items. Their bright colors and easy workability also make them a fun material to customize to match your personal style.  

### Preparing the Foam  

Start by selecting pool noodles in colors and diameters that suit your project. For larger items such as vases, candle holders, or figurines, choose thicker noodles for maximum cushioning. For smaller, more fragile ornaments, thinner noodles or even sections trimmed from a wider noodle will suffice.  

Use a sharp utility knife or heavy-duty scissors to slice the noodle lengthwise, creating an opening to wrap around your item. You can also cut the noodle into shorter segments to fit the height of your décor piece. If you need a snug fit, trim away small slivers until the foam hugs the surface of the object without compressing it too tightly.  

### Crafting Sleeves for Home Décor  

For delicate home décor such as porcelain figurines, glassware, or hand-carved wooden pieces, foam sleeves help prevent chips and cracks. Measure the circumference of your item, then cut the noodle lengthwise and hollow out the inner channel slightly to accommodate any irregular shapes. Slip the sleeve over the item, ensuring the foam covers all vulnerable edges.  

If you’re storing multiple items together, consider adding a layer of fabric around the foam for extra softness and to prevent color transfer. You can stitch or glue the fabric in place, turning a utilitarian sleeve into a decorative storage accessory.  

### Holiday Ornament Protection  

Holiday ornaments—whether made of glass, ceramic, or other fragile materials—often require special care during storage. By cutting pool noodles into short rings, you can create individual ornament holders. Simply slice the ring open, insert the ornament, and close it back up. The foam will cradle the ornament, keeping it secure inside a larger storage box.  

For oddly shaped ornaments, use a combination of foam pieces to create custom contours. Hot glue can be applied sparingly to join foam segments together, forming a tailored protective shell. This method works well for heirloom ornaments with intricate designs that don’t fit standard storage compartments.  

### Adding Creative Flair  

Protective sleeves don’t have to be plain. Use acrylic paint or fabric wraps to match the sleeves to your décor theme. For holiday storage, you might decorate the foam with festive ribbon or stickers, making the process of unpacking ornaments each year more enjoyable. For everyday décor, neutral tones or patterned fabric covers can help the sleeves blend seamlessly with your storage area.  

### Beyond Protection  

Once you’ve mastered making foam sleeves, the same technique can be applied to other uses: cushioning tools, protecting electronics during travel, or even creating grips for sports equipment. The adaptability of pool noodles means that one simple material can serve dozens of purposes throughout your home.  

### Final Thoughts  

Repurposing foam pool noodles into protective sleeves is a cost-effective and creative way to safeguard cherished items. With minimal tools and a bit of imagination, you can transform these summertime staples into year-round helpers. Whether you’re preserving holiday ornaments or shielding delicate décor, foam sleeves offer a customizable solution that combines functionality with fun.  

By embracing the versatility of pool noodles, you not only protect your possessions but also engage in a satisfying DIY craft that lets you tailor every detail to your needs and style. So, gather your materials, clear a workspace, and start cutting—your treasures will thank you for the extra care.

**Backyard Propane Fire Pits: Design Trends and Safety Essentials**  

There’s something timeless about gathering around a warm flame in the comfort of your own backyard. In recent years, decorative propane-fueled fire pits have surged in popularity, blending the ambiance of traditional campfires with modern convenience and safety. Homeowners are increasingly seeking designs that not only elevate outdoor aesthetics but also provide a focal point for social gatherings. Below, we explore the latest design trends, optimal placement strategies, and crucial safety guidelines for installing and maintaining these features.  

---

### **Design Trends Shaping Backyard Fire Pits**  

**Minimalist and Modern Lines**  
Contemporary outdoor spaces often favor clean, geometric shapes. Square or rectangular propane fire tables with sleek finishes—such as powder-coated steel, concrete composite, or tempered glass accents—are replacing rustic round pits in many suburban yards. These designs coordinate seamlessly with modern patio furniture and outdoor kitchens, creating a cohesive look.  

**Mixed Materials for Visual Interest**  
Designers are combining materials like natural stone veneers, reclaimed wood mantels, and ceramic tiles to create texture and depth. A propane burner can be housed in a structure that doubles as a coffee table when the flame is off, maximizing functionality.  

**Integrated Seating and Lighting**  
Permanent seating installations—such as curved benches or sectional sofas—are being built around fire pits to encourage conversation and comfort. LED strip lighting under seating or along pathways enhances the ambiance and extends usability into the night.  

**Custom Burner Arrangements**  
Advances in burner technology allow for unique flame patterns, from linear troughs to circular rings, giving homeowners the ability to personalize the fire’s visual impact. Some setups incorporate colored fire glass or lava rock for added sparkle and heat distribution.  

---

### **Placement for Social Flow and Safety**  

A propane fire pit should be positioned to optimize both the view and the flow of movement. Consider these placement tips:  

- **Central Gathering Spot:** Situate the pit in a location that naturally draws people together, such as the center of a patio or between distinct seating zones.  
- **Clearance from Structures:** Maintain a safe distance—typically at least 7 to 10 feet—from walls, fences, and overhanging branches. This prevents heat damage and reduces fire risk.  
- **Wind Considerations:** Place the pit in a spot sheltered from prevailing winds to avoid flame distortion and improve comfort for guests.  
- **Sightlines:** Align the fire pit so that it can be viewed from multiple angles, including indoor spaces, to create a visual connection between indoors and outdoors.  

---

### **Safety Guidelines for Installation and Operation**  

While propane fire pits are considered safer than wood-burning alternatives due to controlled ignition and reduced sparks, proper installation and maintenance are essential.  

**Professional Setup**  
Always have a certified technician connect the propane supply, whether it’s a direct line from a home tank or a portable cylinder. Proper fittings and leak tests are critical to prevent hazards.  

**Ventilation and Surface Stability**  
Ensure adequate ventilation beneath and around the burner to avoid gas buildup. The fire pit should be installed on a level, non-combustible surface such as stone pavers or concrete.  

**Routine Maintenance**  
Inspect burners and ignition systems regularly for debris or corrosion. Clean fire glass or lava rock to maintain flame quality. Replace any worn hoses or fittings immediately.  

**Safe Operation Practices**  
Keep flammable materials away from the flame, and never leave the fire unattended. Use the manufacturer’s recommended cover when the pit is not in use to protect components from weather and animals.  

---

### **Enhancing the Experience**  

To create a truly inviting atmosphere, consider pairing your propane fire pit with complementary outdoor elements:  

- **Weather-Resistant Lounge Furniture:** Cushioned chairs and sofas with fade-resistant fabrics encourage longer gatherings.  
- **Outdoor Rugs:** Define the space visually and add comfort underfoot.  
- **Seasonal Decor:** Lanterns, planters, and throw blankets can be rotated to match the season and enhance the mood.  
- **Soundscapes:** Discreet outdoor speakers can provide background music, while the crackle of a flame remains the centerpiece.  

---

Propane-fueled fire pits offer a blend of style, convenience, and safety that appeals to a wide range of homeowners. By thoughtfully selecting designs, placing them for optimal social interaction, and adhering to safety guidelines, you can create an outdoor space that becomes the heart of your home year-round. Whether for quiet evenings or lively gatherings, the right fire feature can make your backyard a destination in itself.

**Report on Emerging Trends in Synthetic Lubricants for Heavy Machinery: Performance Enhancement and Environmental Impact**  

---

**Abstract**  
The industrial sector faces increasing demands for machinery performance, operational efficiency, and environmental compliance. Synthetic lubricants, developed through advanced petrochemical formulations, have emerged as a critical component in meeting these requirements. This report examines recent innovations in synthetic lubricant production, focusing on their ability to reduce wear and tear, extend service intervals, and mitigate environmental impact. Developments in base stock chemistry, additive technology, and lifecycle management are analyzed alongside regulatory pressures and market trends.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Lubricants are fundamental to the operation of heavy machinery, ensuring smooth function, minimizing friction, and preventing premature component failure. Traditional mineral-based lubricants, while effective in certain applications, are increasingly challenged by performance limitations and environmental concerns. Synthetic lubricants—engineered from chemically modified petrochemical base stocks—offer superior stability, tailored viscosity profiles, and reduced volatility. Recent advances in production methodologies have allowed manufacturers to create formulations that simultaneously enhance mechanical efficiency and align with emerging sustainability standards.

---

**2. Advances in Base Stock Formulation**  
Synthetic lubricants are commonly derived from polyalphaolefins (PAOs), esters, and other engineered hydrocarbons. Innovations in molecular design have enabled greater control over viscosity index, thermal stability, and oxidation resistance. For example, new PAO variants with optimized chain lengths exhibit improved film strength under extreme pressures, reducing metal-to-metal contact and extending component life. Ester-based synthetics now incorporate branched molecular structures that enhance lubricity and biodegradability, addressing both performance and environmental priorities.

---

**3. Additive Technology Developments**  
Additives are integral to lubricant efficacy, providing anti-wear, anti-oxidation, and corrosion protection. Recent research has produced ashless anti-wear agents that minimize particulate emissions during operation. Advanced detergents and dispersants maintain cleanliness in hydraulic systems and gearboxes, reducing sludge formation and maintaining efficiency over prolonged service periods. Friction modifiers based on molybdenum or organic compounds are being refined to function effectively under high-load, high-temperature conditions without compromising environmental compliance.

---

**4. Environmental Considerations**  
The environmental footprint of lubricants is shaped by their production, usage, and disposal. Emerging synthetic formulations are increasingly designed for reduced toxicity, improved biodegradability, and lower greenhouse gas emissions during manufacture. Lifecycle assessments indicate that extended drain intervals—made possible by the superior stability of synthetics—substantially decrease lubricant consumption and waste generation. Regulatory frameworks such as the EU Ecolabel and ISO 14024 Type I environmental labeling are influencing product development, encouraging manufacturers to adopt renewable feedstocks and closed-loop recycling systems.

---

**5. Performance in Heavy Machinery Applications**  
In mining, construction, and agricultural machinery, synthetic lubricants have demonstrated measurable benefits in reducing downtime and maintenance costs. High-load gear systems benefit from enhanced film strength and shear stability, while hydraulic systems operate more efficiently due to reduced fluid degradation. Field studies show that synthetic lubricants can extend component life by 20–40% compared to conventional oils, primarily through reduced wear rates and superior thermal control. This has direct implications for operational productivity and cost management in industries reliant on continuous heavy machinery operation.

---

**6. Production Trends and Market Outlook**  
Global demand for synthetic lubricants is projected to grow at a compound annual rate exceeding 5% over the next decade, driven by industrial modernization and stricter environmental regulations. Manufacturers are investing in catalytic synthesis processes that reduce energy consumption and emissions during lubricant production. Collaborative research between petrochemical companies and machinery OEMs is fostering customized lubricant solutions tailored to specific operating environments, further enhancing efficiency and sustainability.

---

**7. Conclusion**  
Synthetic lubricants represent a significant advancement in heavy machinery maintenance and performance optimization. Through innovation in base stock chemistry, additive composition, and environmentally conscious production, these formulations deliver extended service life, reduced mechanical wear, and compliance with evolving sustainability standards. As industrial sectors continue to prioritize efficiency and environmental stewardship, synthetic lubricants are poised to play an increasingly central role in machinery operation strategies.

---

over time. Compared to prior decades, fatality rates have declined significantly because of
technological improvements, as well as behavioral shifts, such as increased seat belt use. As
these safer vehicles replace older less safe vehicles in the fleet, the on-road fleet is replaced with
vehicles reflecting the improved fatality rates of newer, safer vehicles. However, fatality rates
associated with different model year vehicles are influenced by the vehicle itself and by driver
behavior. Over time, used vehicles are purchased by drivers in different demographic
circumstances who also tend to have different behavioral characteristics. Data from the Fatality
Analysis Reporting System (FARS) indicate that drivers of older vehicles, on average, tend to
have lower belt use rates, are more likely to drive inebriated, and are more likely to drive over
the speed limit. Additionally, older vehicles are more likely to be driven on rural roadways,

Finally, wood is an important source of material and energy for much of the world. Trees that are cut down in cities or communities can be used for timber (Sherrill, 2003). This could be used for fuel or for producing goods. Innovative programs can promote sustainability and creative usage of urban wood. An example of this is the “Working for Water” program which trains people in South Africa to remove woody invasive species, and then the cleared wood can be used for a variety of secondary industries (Binns, Illgner, & Nel, 2001). While this program works with invasive species, it serves as an example of creative solutions involving the community with urban issues involving trees. Urban forests can also help supply affordable energy to people that need it (FAO, 2016). It is important to note, however, that burning wood is a large contributor to air pollution in urban environments (Favez, Cachier, Sciare, Sarda-Estève, & Martinon, 2009). Therefore, if wood is used for fuel, it should be burned in such a way that the benefits outweigh the harm to human health. Trees are a valuable resource, even after they are cut down.

Over 2.3 billion years ago, early cyanobacteria began emitting O2 via photosynthesis (Kasting and Siefert 2002). Considering that the earth’s atmosphere stabilized at ~21% O2 and ~78% nitrogen (N2) about 550 million years ago (Berner 1999), it is safe to say that modern humans evolved to efficiently use this atmosphere for “normal” breathing (Liem 1988).

**Historical Trends in Decorative Motifs in Wooden, Ceramic, and Metal Artifacts, 18th–20th Centuries**  

---

**Abstract**  
This study investigates the evolution of decorative motifs applied to wooden, ceramic, and metal artifacts between the 18th and 20th centuries, emphasizing the aesthetic preferences and cultural symbolism embedded within these materials. By tracing stylistic shifts across three major periods—the late Baroque and Rococo of the 18th century, the neoclassical and industrial expansion of the 19th century, and the modernist and revivalist movements of the early to mid-20th century—this paper identifies recurring themes, regional variations, and the interplay between technological innovation and artistic expression. The analysis draws on museum collections, archival records, and contemporary treatises to highlight how motifs functioned as carriers of identity, status, and ideological values.  

---

**Introduction**  
Decorative motifs serve as a visual language through which societies articulate aesthetic ideals, cultural affiliations, and symbolic narratives. Between the 18th and 20th centuries, artisans working with wood, ceramics, and metals developed and adapted motif repertoires in response to shifting tastes, global trade, and advances in manufacturing techniques. While the functional qualities of these materials differed markedly, their surfaces offered artists and craftsmen opportunities to explore analogous themes—floral ornamentation, geometric patterning, heraldic emblems, and allegorical imagery—within distinct cultural contexts.  

This paper examines three chronological phases, situating motifs within broader socio-cultural movements and considering the influence of cross-cultural contact, industrialization, and the rise of mass production on design vocabulary.

---

**18th Century: Late Baroque and Rococo Flourishes**  
In the 18th century, wooden furniture and decorative panels often featured intricate carving in high relief, incorporating acanthus leaves, shells, and scrollwork emblematic of Rococo exuberance [1]. Ceramics of the period, particularly porcelain from Meissen and Sèvres, displayed hand-painted pastoral scenes and floral sprays, frequently framed by gilded borders. Metal artifacts—such as silver serving ware and bronze candelabra—were embellished with repoussé and chasing techniques to produce similar organic forms, underscoring a shared ornamental lexicon across materials.  

Cultural symbolism in this era leaned heavily toward courtly refinement and controlled asymmetry, with motifs reinforcing aristocratic ideals of leisure, harmony with nature, and cosmopolitan sophistication. The exchange of designs between workshops in France, England, and Central Europe illustrates the interconnectedness of decorative trends.

---

**19th Century: Neoclassicism and Industrial Ornament**  
The early 19th century witnessed a turn toward neoclassical motifs, inspired by archaeological discoveries in Pompeii and Herculaneum. Wooden furniture adopted cleaner lines, symmetrical arrangements, and motifs such as laurel wreaths, Greek key patterns, and mythological figures. Ceramics incorporated transfer-printed scenes of antiquity, enabling broader dissemination of classical imagery to middle-class consumers.  

Metalwork, including wrought iron and cast brass, embraced both classical and emerging industrial decorative vocabularies. Advances in casting allowed for precise repetition of motifs such as palmettes and anthemia, while also introducing new machine-derived patterns. The symbolism of the neoclassical style conveyed ideals of rational order, civic virtue, and continuity with ancient civilizations [2]. By the mid-century, however, the Gothic Revival and Orientalist trends diversified motif repertoires, blending historicist references with exotic elements drawn from increased global contact.

---

**20th Century: Modernism and Revivalism**  
The early 20th century brought radical shifts in decorative aesthetics. Modernist movements such as Art Deco and Bauhaus advocated geometric simplification, stylized natural forms, and a reduction of ornament to essential lines. Wooden artifacts, including chairs and cabinetry, often featured veneered surfaces with inlaid abstract patterns or streamlined contours. Ceramics adopted bold color blocking, angular motifs, and stylized flora, reflecting the influence of cubism and contemporary graphic arts.  

Metal artifacts, particularly in architectural and interior contexts, showcased chrome plating, machine-turned textures, and repetitive geometric reliefs. The symbolism in modernist motifs often aligned with ideals of progress, efficiency, and a break from historicist traditions.  

Simultaneously, revivalist movements such as the Colonial Revival in North America and the Arts and Crafts Movement in Britain reintroduced traditional motifs—hand-carved floral designs in wood, slip-trailed botanical patterns in ceramics, and hammered metalwork with medieval or folk-inspired imagery—imbued with nostalgia and a desire to reaffirm cultural heritage [3].

---

**Conclusion**  
Across the 18th to 20th centuries, decorative motifs in wooden, ceramic, and metal artifacts both mirrored and shaped prevailing aesthetic values. Despite differences in material properties and production methods, artisans frequently engaged with shared visual themes, adapting them to suit contemporary tastes and symbolic needs. The interplay between tradition and innovation, local identity and global exchange, ensured that motifs retained their capacity to convey meaning while evolving in form and execution.  

---

[2] Honour, H. *Neoclassicism*. London: Penguin, 1981.  
[3] Naylor, G. *The Arts and Crafts Movement: A Study of Its Sources, Ideals and Influence on Design Theory*. London: Studio Vista, 1971.

**Report: Advancements in Low-Temperature Cooking Appliances for Commercial Kitchens**  

---

**Abstract**  
Recent developments in induction-based simmering systems have introduced new opportunities for energy efficiency and quality control in commercial kitchen operations. This report examines the engineering innovations behind low-temperature cooking appliances, with a focus on safety feature validation, airflow optimization, and the integration of smart fan systems to ensure uniform heat distribution. Laboratory and field tests demonstrate that these systems can maintain consistent food quality while reducing overall energy consumption.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
Commercial kitchens face increasing demands for energy-efficient equipment that does not compromise food quality. Traditional high-temperature cooking methods often result in uneven heating and higher energy costs. Low-temperature cooking appliances, particularly those employing induction-based simmering, present a viable alternative. These systems operate at controlled temperatures, reducing thermal stress on both food and equipment, while incorporating active airflow management to enhance performance.  

---

**2. Technology Overview**  
The core of modern low-temperature cooking appliances lies in precision induction heating elements. Unlike resistive heating plates, induction systems generate heat directly within the cooking vessel through electromagnetic fields, allowing for rapid adjustments and stable temperature profiles. The simmering mode typically operates between 60°C and 95°C, suitable for delicate preparations such as sauces, slow-cooked proteins, and custards.  

Key to the performance of these systems is the incorporation of thin-profile heating plates with optimized airflow channels. A network of embedded sensors monitors plate temperature and surface conditions, feeding data to a central control unit. Smart fan assemblies, positioned strategically around the heating zone, modulate airflow to ensure even heat distribution across the cooking surface.  

---

**3. Safety Feature Testing**  
Safety is paramount in commercial kitchens. The induction-based simmering systems undergo rigorous testing to meet compliance standards for thermal safety, electrical integrity, and operator protection. Automatic shut-off mechanisms engage when sensors detect abnormal temperature spikes or airflow obstructions.  

Fire risk is mitigated through cool-touch surfaces and low ambient heat emission, reducing the chance of accidental burns or ignition of nearby materials. Additionally, airflow pathways are designed to resist grease buildup, which can otherwise impair cooling efficiency and create hazards over time.  

---

**4. Airflow Optimization**  
Uniform temperature distribution across the cooking surface is essential for consistent food quality. Engineers have implemented computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations to design airflow channels that minimize turbulence while maximizing convective heat transfer.  

Fan systems are typically comprised of low-wattage, high-efficiency units, each capable of variable speed control. By synchronizing fan activity with real-time sensor data, the system compensates for localized temperature drops or hotspots, achieving a near-constant thermal environment. This is particularly beneficial for multi-vessel setups, where each cooking zone requires precise thermal regulation.  

---

**5. Energy Consumption and Efficiency Gains**  
Low-temperature induction simmering systems consume significantly less energy compared to traditional gas or resistive electric appliances. The reduced operating temperature lowers thermal losses to the surrounding environment, while the direct heating method minimizes the time needed to reach target temperatures.  

Energy monitoring during pilot installations in commercial kitchens indicates reductions in electricity usage of 10–15% over comparable output scenarios with conventional appliances. Smart fan modulation further contributes to savings by reducing airflow power when thermal stability is achieved, without compromising uniform heat distribution.  

---

**6. Integration into Commercial Operations**  
Deployment of these systems requires minimal adaptation from kitchen staff, as control interfaces are designed to be intuitive. Preset programs for common low-temperature recipes simplify operation and reduce training time. Maintenance routines are streamlined through modular fan assemblies and accessible airflow channels, enabling rapid cleaning and servicing.  

The compact form factor of induction simmering units allows for integration into existing cooking lines without major reconfiguration. This flexibility supports phased adoption, enabling operators to trial the technology in specific stations before committing to full-scale implementation.  

---

**7. Conclusion**  
Low-temperature induction-based simmering appliances represent a significant advancement in commercial kitchen technology. By combining precise temperature control, optimized airflow, and smart fan integration, these systems deliver consistent food quality with measurable energy savings. Safety features and ease of integration further enhance their suitability for modern culinary environments. Continued refinement of airflow designs and control algorithms is expected to yield even greater efficiency and performance in the coming years.  

---

**End of Report**

**Cleaner Rails Ahead: How Electric Train Innovations Are Cutting Emissions**  

In recent years, the rail industry has seen a surge in investment and research aimed at reducing the environmental footprint of train travel. While trains have long been considered more efficient than road or air transport, the reliance on diesel locomotives in many regions has continued to contribute to air pollution, particularly in and around busy stations. Now, new electric propulsion systems are reshaping the conversation, offering cleaner, quieter, and more sustainable mobility for urban and intercity passengers.  

**From Diesel to Electric: A Shift in Propulsion**  

Traditional diesel-powered locomotives generate emissions both from engine exhaust and wear-related particulate matter. These pollutants—ranging from nitrogen oxides to ultrafine particles—can accumulate in enclosed or semi-enclosed station environments, posing health concerns for commuters and staff. Electric trains, by contrast, operate without onboard combustion, meaning they produce no direct exhaust at the point of use.  

The adoption of electric propulsion is not new, but recent advancements have made these systems more efficient, lighter, and easier to integrate into existing rail networks. High-efficiency traction motors, regenerative braking systems, and improved inverter technology have allowed electric trains to consume less energy while delivering higher performance.  

**Advancements in Energy Efficiency**  

One of the most significant breakthroughs has come from the development of permanent magnet synchronous motors (PMSMs), which offer greater torque density and efficiency compared to traditional induction motors. Coupled with smart control algorithms, these motors enable smoother acceleration and deceleration, reducing energy waste and mechanical strain.  

Regenerative braking—a technology that captures kinetic energy during deceleration and feeds it back into the grid or onboard storage—has also matured. Modern systems recover up to 30% of the energy otherwise lost as heat, directly lowering the overall electricity demand of a rail service.  

**Reducing Operational Emissions**  

While electric trains themselves produce no tailpipe emissions, the environmental benefit depends on the source of the electricity. Regions that draw heavily on renewable energy see the greatest reductions in lifecycle emissions. Even in areas reliant on fossil fuels, electric trains tend to outperform diesel in terms of total pollutants released per passenger-kilometre.  

Station air quality also improves markedly when electric trains replace diesel units. Without the exhaust plumes from idling engines, concentrations of harmful gases and particulates drop, making platforms and concourses healthier spaces. This is particularly important in underground or partially enclosed stations where ventilation is limited.  

**Design Innovations for Cleaner Operation**  

Manufacturers are incorporating aerodynamic improvements, lightweight composite materials, and modular battery packs into new train designs. Some models are capable of operating in hybrid mode—drawing power from overhead lines where available and switching to battery reserves in non-electrified segments. This flexibility reduces the need for diesel backup locomotives, further cutting emissions.  

Noise pollution is also reduced with electric operation. Quieter trains lessen the stress on passengers and nearby communities, contributing to a more comfortable travel experience and a smaller environmental impact.  

**Global Adoption and Policy Support**  

Countries across Europe and Asia have accelerated electrification projects, spurred by both climate commitments and public health concerns. In the UK, for example, government-backed initiatives aim to phase out diesel-only trains by the mid-2040s. Japan’s Shinkansen network has long been a model for high-speed electric rail, demonstrating the potential for efficient, low-emission long-distance travel.  

Emerging economies are also investing heavily in electric rail infrastructure, recognizing its role in reducing urban air pollution. India’s railways have set ambitious targets to fully electrify their network within the next decade, while China continues to expand its already extensive high-speed electric rail system.  

**Looking Ahead**  

The trajectory of rail transport points toward widespread electrification, supported by ongoing innovation in propulsion technology, energy recovery, and sustainable materials. As these systems become more efficient and cost-effective, the environmental and health benefits will grow, making electric trains a cornerstone of cleaner public transportation.  

For commuters and policymakers alike, the shift to modern electric rail represents more than just an upgrade in technology—it is a step toward a future where mobility is both efficient and environmentally responsible. The continued refinement of these systems promises not only reduced emissions but also improved air quality in stations, cities, and communities served by the railway network.

**Title:**  
Ecological Benefits of Ornamental Perennial Plantings in Urban Landscapes: Mitigation of Heat Island Effects and Air Quality Improvement  

---

**Abstract**  
Urban environments are characterized by elevated temperatures and degraded air quality due to high concentrations of impervious surfaces and anthropogenic emissions. This paper investigates the ecological impact of integrating ornamental perennial species into urban landscapes, with emphasis on their capacity to reduce urban heat island (UHI) intensity and enhance atmospheric quality. Drawing on recent empirical studies, the analysis explores the physiological and morphological traits of selected perennials that contribute to microclimatic regulation and pollutant mitigation. The findings indicate that strategic deployment of ornamental perennials in densely populated areas can yield measurable environmental benefits, reinforcing their role in sustainable urban planning.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Urbanization has led to significant alterations in local climate systems, notably through the emergence of the urban heat island phenomenon, wherein metropolitan cores experience higher ambient temperatures than surrounding rural regions [1]. Elevated temperatures exacerbate energy demand, increase pollutant formation rates, and pose health risks to urban residents. Concurrently, air quality in cities is often compromised by particulate matter (PM), nitrogen oxides (NOₓ), and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Urban green infrastructure, particularly vegetation, has been recognized as a viable approach to ameliorating these challenges [2]. While trees are frequently cited as primary agents of climate moderation, ornamental perennial plants represent an underutilized resource with potential to contribute significantly to UHI mitigation and air purification.

---

**2. Ornamental Perennials and Microclimatic Regulation**  
Perennial plants, defined by their multi-year life cycle, present several ecological advantages in urban contexts. Their persistent root systems improve soil structure, enhance water infiltration, and reduce surface runoff. Aboveground, dense foliage and varied canopy structures intercept solar radiation, leading to localized cooling effects through shading and evapotranspiration [3]. Species such as *Echinacea purpurea* and *Rudbeckia fulgida* have demonstrated high leaf area indices (LAI), which correlate positively with reductions in surface and air temperatures in landscaped plots [4].

The seasonal stability of perennials ensures consistent microclimatic benefits throughout the growing season, unlike annuals whose effects are temporally limited. Furthermore, the diversity of morphological forms among ornamental perennials—ranging from low groundcovers to taller herbaceous species—allows for tiered planting schemes that maximize shading efficiency and airflow modulation.

---

**3. Air Quality Enhancement Mechanisms**  
Vegetation influences air quality through both direct and indirect mechanisms. Directly, plant surfaces capture airborne particulates, while stomatal uptake facilitates the removal of gaseous pollutants such as ozone (O₃) and NOₓ [5]. Ornamental perennials with pubescent leaves or textured surfaces, such as *Stachys byzantina*, exhibit enhanced particulate capture capacity. Indirectly, cooling effects from vegetation can reduce the photochemical formation of ground-level ozone by lowering ambient temperatures, thereby slowing reaction rates between precursor pollutants.

Additionally, perennial vegetation contributes to soil microbial activity that can further degrade certain airborne contaminants deposited on surfaces. The perennial root-soil interface supports rhizosphere communities capable of metabolizing organic pollutants, thus integrating air quality improvement into broader biogeochemical cycles.

---

**4. Strategic Urban Deployment**  
Maximizing the ecological benefits of ornamental perennials requires careful spatial planning. Planting schemes should prioritize high-exposure zones, such as south-facing building facades and open plazas, where heat accumulation is greatest. Clusters of perennials can be integrated into median strips, pocket parks, and rooftop gardens to extend cooling and filtration services across the urban fabric [6]. Species selection must account for local climate conditions, pollutant profiles, and maintenance constraints to ensure long-term viability.

Mixed-species plantings can enhance resilience against pests and diseases while broadening ecological functions. For example, combining drought-tolerant perennials with species that exhibit high pollutant uptake can address multiple environmental stressors simultaneously. Seasonal flowering patterns also contribute to urban biodiversity by supporting pollinator populations.

---

**5. Conclusion**  
Ornamental perennials represent a versatile and sustainable component of urban green infrastructure. Their capacity to reduce heat island intensity through shading and evapotranspiration, alongside their role in capturing airborne particulates and absorbing gaseous pollutants, underscores their relevance to climate-responsive city design. Integrating ornamental perennials into urban landscapes can yield measurable improvements in microclimate regulation and air quality, fostering healthier, more livable environments.

---

# Quantifying Methane Emissions from Landfilled Food Waste Methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, is emitted from landfills, resulting from the decaying of organic waste over time under anaerobic conditions. Municipal solid waste landfills are the third-largest source of methane emissions from human activities in the United States. Food waste comprises about 24 percent of municipal solid waste disposed of in landfills. Due to its quick decay rate, food waste in landfills is contributing to more methane emissions than any other landfilled materials. An estimated 58 percent of the fugitive methane emissions (i.e., those released to the atmosphere) from municipal solid waste landfills are from landfilled food waste. ## Report To understand the impact food waste has on U.S. landfill greenhouse gas emissions, EPA developed the report, _Quantifying Methane Emissions from Landfilled Food Waste_, to estimate the quantity of methane emissions released into the atmosphere from decaying food waste in municipal solid waste landfills in the United States from 1990 to 2020. This analysis relied on existing, widely-used EPA models and data sources to compare the estimates of modeled methane emissions while examining factors that influence methane emissions. These factors include 1) total tonnage of landfilled food waste, 2) landfill characteristics, 3) food waste decay rate, 4) landfill gas collection systems installation and efficiency, and 5) amount of methane oxidized as the gas passes through the landfill cover material. This report is EPA’s first published estimate of annual methane emissions from landfilled food waste and the first peer-reviewed national reference point for the amount of methane emissions attributable to food waste in U.S. municipal solid waste landfills. Results from the analysis revealed that while total emissions from municipal solid waste landfills are decreasing, methane emissions from landfilled food waste are increasing. Findings from this report illustrate the outsized impact landfilled food waste has on methane emissions. This data confirms that diverting food waste from landfills is an effective way to reduce methane emissions from municipal solid waste landfills. ## Calculator While developing the report, EPA recognized the need for a calculator that interested parties can use to estimate the total avoided methane emissions per ton of food waste diverted from final disposal in landfills over time. The Avoided Landfilled Food Waste Methane Emissions Calculator uses the same landfill and food waste characteristics found in the “Quantifying Methane Emissions from Landfilled Food Waste” report (e.g., food waste decay rate, food waste’s methane generation potential) and uses factors from the EPA Waste Reduction Model (WARM) (e.g., methane destruction efficiency in flares, methane collection efficiency, gas collection installation schedule) to estimate the amount of methane generated from each ton of landfilled food waste. The calculator can be used by anyone, including state, Tribal, and local governments, institutions, schools, or private companies, to estimate the methane emissions reductions per ton of food waste that does not go to the landfill. Users can download the calculator and use the results for their own outcomes, including grant applications, program planning, and reporting.

Heat load control is the key to an efficient multiple boiler strategy. Here are the main points to consider. Traditional temperature-based control strategies are almost universally used for boiler sequence control. However, although limitations have been known for many years, they are often ignored. Here, we look at how strategies based on heat load, rather than temperature, can provide more stable control and effi cient operation. Most modern boilers, and some older ones, are more effi cient at low loads than at high loads, yet most traditional sequence control systems modulate one boiler up to full output, followed by the next boiler, and so on. Improvement in efficiency at lower loads varies depending on the boiler, but is typically around 3%. Condensing boilers are more effi cient, with low return water temperatures, but unless the return water temperature is below 54° C, they do not work in condensing mode. Maximum condensing operation does not occur until return temperatures are as low as 30° C, which can further increase efficiency by up to 8%. However, the mean temperatures necessary for most heat emitters normally preclude return temperatures that are quite so low. ## HWS segregation This offers many advantages in most buildings. Condensing boilers can be operated at lower temperatures, or directly compensated more easily where HWS is independent of heating. Pumping and standing losses are also reduced where heating boilers are shut down in summer. HWS can be supplied by point-of-use water heaters, or by condensing gas-fired instantaneous/semi-storage units where demands are greater. ## Traditional boiler sequence control systems Traditional multiple boilers, controlled from the boiler primary circuit flow or return temperature, are often unstable or ineffectively controlled. Control from return temperature is generally considered to be more stable, but can only be used where the primary flow is constant, as the return temperature is only representative of the load in such circumstances. This is still poorly understood by many system designers. Flow-temperature sequence control can be effective with boilers that have modulating burners and individual pumps. Many modern boilers have a 0-10V control function, which permits either direct modulating control of the burners, or setpoint reset for direct compensation of the boiler. Where direct modulating control of the burner is used, the individual boiler controls should comply with BS EN 15502-1: 2012 for gas-fired boilers, and should limit the maximum outlet temperature via burner modulation to a safe margin below the high limit temperature, regardless of the 0-10V signal. Many packaged boiler controls use PID control loops that are pre-set to provide the most consistent burner modulation under all load conditions. Flow-temperature sequence control must allow for pumps/boilers being started and stopped, with stable control requiring careful commissioning. It is also possible to set up the output stages of flow temperature sequence control to provide more efficient operation. However, poor commissioning of flow temperature sequence control is common, and frequently ends up with all boilers operating continuously. An increase in proportional band and integral action time rapidly provides stable operation, but this might never be noticed without appropriate witnessing of commissioning. Flow-temperature sequence control setpoints should be slightly lower than the boiler setpoint (or compensated) to avoid interaction between the sequence control and the boiler controls. ## Heat load control Heat load is calculated from flow and return temperatures and flow rate (Q=MC°t), or via a heat meter which has an analogue heat output in kW. Most modern building management systems can calculate Q=MC°t, so heat meters are not necessary, but can be used. Magnetic flow meters are considered to be the most accurate and to have the greatest turndown. Ultrasonic are more common and normally used, for example, as an inherent part of heat meters for Renewable Heat Incentive (RHI) applications. Magnetic and RHI heat meters are insertion meters, while clamp-on ultrasonic meters are also available. Clamp-on meters are less accurate than insertion meters, but flexibility to relocate to the correct location can be beneficial. Generally the minimum straight length of pipe is 10D upstream and 5D downstream. This needs to be of the same ID as the flow meter for insertion meters. Some ultrasonic flow meters ideally require 20D upstream and 10D downstream, but generally have been found to be sufficiently accurate with 10D/5D for heat load control purposes. CJ ## Benefits and downsides of heat flow control Advantages of heat load control include: - More stable operation of boilers, particularly at low load - More efficient operation of boilers, as control can be set in accordance with the most economic operation of the boiler, which is normally at low load above minimum fire - No risk of interaction between temperature settings of boilers and sequence control, which frequently causes ineffective flowtemperature sequence control - Effective control of high/low fire boilers is possible - Effective control of combinations of different sizes/types of boiler - Effective control where boilers do not reach their rated outlet temperatures - Normally more rapid and effective commissioning - Boilers are only enabled by the heat load control; therefore the stable firing of the boiler is entirely the boiler supplier's responsibility - Direct boiler compensation (reset of setpoint via 0-10v signal) can be incorporated, improving condensing operation - Often the only effective method of control of bivalent systems. Disadvantages include: - Additional capital cost, but this is paid back with long-term effective control - The systems integrators need to understand the principles of operation and take account of the factors that are essential for effective heat load control. - And the following factors are essential for effective heat load control: - Flow meters must be correctly located and commissioned - Matched flow and return temperature sensors are required - The lead boiler should be enabled according to demand (or optimum start), as there is no load detected on system start-up when flow and return temperatures are equal. The lag, or subsequent, boilers are enabled according to heat load - The boiler is normally controlled via its packaged controls, with respect to boiler outlet temperature

Removing all the mass from Earth's core and leaving only the mantle and crust would have a significant effect on the gravitational pull of the Earth. By removing this mass, the gravitational force experienced by objects on the surface of the Earth would be considerably reduced.

**Heavy-duty electric trucks show impressive consumption figures on flat routes and under optimal conditions: with light goods, values of around 90 kWh per 100 kilometers can be achieved – that corresponds to around 9.2 liters of diesel. But the reality is often different. In this article, you will find out how much energy electric trucks actually consume in different applications. The data comes from the fleet monitoring of 239 Designwerk customer vehicles and provides valuable insights into practice.** Whether diesel or electric vehicle – the main factors influencing energy consumption remain the same: distance, weight, topography, driving style, road and weather conditions as well as the specific area of use. These factors could not be more different in our customers’ applications. As an expert in electric trucks for special applications, we supply everything from sewer cleaning vehicles to long-distance transporters. Two extremes: energy consumption in practice -------------------------------------------- Our detailed data analysis shows how different consumption can be in different applications. Two impressive examples: ### Sewer cleaning An all-electric sewer cleaner travels around 6,000 kilometers a year, consuming an average of over 360 kWh per 100 kilometers. However, the majority of this energy is not used for driving, but for operating the powerful flushing and suction units. ### Distribution and long-distance transport An electric tractor unit with a battery capacity of up to 1,000 kWh and a payload of approx. 40 tons consumes an average of 130 kWh/100 km. Some of our customers achieve impressive mileages with their Designwerk vehicles: The three top performers covered an average of over 186,000 kilometers in 2024, with individual vehicles already exceeding the 500,000 kilometer total mileage mark. The lowest value was recorded by an international trading platform in Germany with just 95 kWh/100 km – an indication of the transportation of large-volume but light goods in the B2C mail order business. Average consumption per vehicle category; 01.01. – 31.12.2024 The data analysis clearly shows that auxiliary drives play a decisive role in overall consumption. Vehicles with energy-intensive units such as concrete drums or high-pressure flushing systems have high consumption levels despite moderate mileage. Another example is our new all-electric snow plow, which went into operation at the end of 2024. Equipped with a front blade, side blade and salt spreader, it consumes an average of around 380 kWh/100 km when clearing snow – a considerable energy saving compared to the diesel version. Comparison with diesel trucks: mileage and CO₂ emissions -------------------------------------------------------- ### More range with the same energy In 2024, our customers covered a total of 8.8 million kilometers with their Designwerk e-trucks, consuming around 13 million kWh of electricity in the process. Diesel trucks would have only covered 2.2 million kilometers with the same amount of energy – almost 75 percent less. In addition, the fuel costs for the shorter distance covered by the diesel-equivalent vehicle would have been almost twice as high. ### 10,000 tons of CO₂ savings per year The battery-electric drive is not only impressive in terms of efficiency, but also in terms of its carbon footprint. The Designwerk customer fleet consumed an average of 147.5 kWh/100 km. By comparison, a diesel truck fleet with comparable applications would have consumed around 40.7 liters/100 km. Overall, our customers were able to save almost 10,000 tons of CO₂ in 2024. From a tank-to-wheel perspective, the electric fleet from Designwerk emits around 6.25 times less CO₂ during operation than an equivalent diesel fleet. This corresponds to a saving of 84 percent of CO₂ emissions. ### Decarbonization made tangible To make these savings tangible: If the weight of the CO₂ emissions saved were converted into an average filled 40-foot container (total weight 6 tons per container), a clear picture would emerge: * Electric truck: 317 containers * Diesel trucks: 1,978 containers Our customers are thus making a significant contribution to the decarbonization of the transport sector.
